response: Two linked reforms would most effectively increase affordable, good-quality homes in my area. First, mandate higher energy standards for all new builds and fund retrofits for older housing to cut bills and meet climate targets without pushing costs onto tenants. This would mean clear requirements for insulation, air-tightness, and efficient heating in new flats, plus grants for upgrading solid-wall homes and shared heating in blocks. In my city there are older council flats that lose heat all winter; reliable retrofit funding could reduce bills by hundreds of pounds a year and make rents feel more affordable over time. Second, encourage purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes with long-term affordability covenants and professional management. This would give renters secure, well-run homes and reduce churn seen in some student housing. A nearby BTR project with an affordability covenant and on-site management stays well maintained and stable, which helps neighbours too. Local authorities could offer planning concessions for schemes that commit to energy efficiency and affordability, with independent oversight to keep standards high.

In my experience here in England, the most effective reforms to boost affordable, good‑quality homes sit at the intersection of smarter land use, targeted specialist housing, and simpler, fair funding mechanisms that recognise local need. Any reform package that ignores the practical realities of older residents, disabled people, students training as key workers, and rural communities risks delivering more high‑rise anecdotes than actual homes. With that in mind, I’d prioritise three linked approaches.

First, raise the standard and depth of disability and care‑ready housing as a norm for affordable homes. I’ve seen households in our town struggle to find homes that are truly adaptable: ground‑floor access, wide doors, zero‑step entry, and the ability to retrofit bathrooms and kitchens without expensive overhauls. It would be sensible to mandate design standards that go beyond minimums—requiring a proportion of affordable homes to be fully wheelchair accessible (M4(3) where practical) and others with flexible layouts to accommodate mobility aids or ageing in place. This should pair with on‑site or near‑site support for older residents, and with clearly defined, scalable options for “additional needs” housing such as sheltered or assisted living linked to local care networks. In our area there’s an aging population but few options that feel like real homes rather than medical facilities; more accessible design and integrated support would reduce the strain on families and local health services.

Second, tailor supply to demographic realities by expanding targeted, community‑based housing delivery—especially for older people, students training as key workers, and those in rural or culturally distinct communities. I’d press for: (a) dedicated schemes for older persons in walkable town centres with access to GP, pharmacy, and social activities; (b) well‑located student key‑worker accommodation near hospitals, universities, and social care training placements to stabilise the local workforce; (c) rural exception sites that respect local character and create affordable options where market housing would otherwise drive prices up. In practice, this means enabling housing associations and trusted not‑for‑profit builders to bring forward mixed‑tenure schemes with robust governance and long‑term affordability. It also means empowering communities to propose and shape projects through local design panels, ensuring new homes suit transport links, schools, and services rather than simply filling a field with bricks.

Third, unlock land at a fair pace and use value capture to fund homes and infrastructure. Releasing surplus public land—e.g., education, health, and local authority sites that sit idle—can kickstart affordable schemes if done transparently and with proper safeguards. The key is to capture some of the uplift in land value created by planning permission and reinvest it in affordable homes, schools, GP surgeries, and transport improvements. A clear, accountable framework for land value capture—whether through a modernised planning uplift levy, a repeatable Infrastructure Levy, or a refreshed version of Section 106 agreements—should ensure communities benefit from new development rather than fund it on the backs of local services. I’d like to see a simple, predictable mechanism that guarantees a portion of uplift goes directly to affordable housing and essential local infrastructure, with ring‑fenced funds for rural transport links and energy efficiency upgrades.

Additionally, reforms must improve delivery speed without compromising quality. Streamlining planning consents for affordable and specialised housing, and creating fast‑track routes for land with proven affordable priorities, would reduce the time between site identification and homes becoming ready to live in. I’d also encourage pilots of modern construction techniques, energy‑efficient standards, and local supply chains to deliver quicker, better‑quality housing with lower running costs for residents.

In practice, the combination of higher accessibility standards, targeted specialist housing, and transparent land value capture could address both the quantity and the quality of affordable homes in my area. The challenge will be ensuring funding is stable, planning reform is clear and predictable, and communities retain a sense of ownership over new developments rather than feeling steamrolled by targets. If these reforms are implemented with robust local oversight, clear governance of uplift, and guaranteed support services for older and disabled residents, they could make a meaningful difference to households who currently struggle to find suitable and affordable accommodation close to work, schools, and care networks.

Agree. For our area, the main barrier to affordable, good-quality homes is the slow planning process rather than a lack of demand. If we streamline planning, zoning and decision timelines while keeping environmental safeguards, housing delivery will speed up and reduce uncertainty for builders. 

I’d back a clear, online planning system with a single pre-application process, standardised forms and a target decision window—ideally 8–12 weeks for straightforward schemes. Allow Permission in Principle on well-located brownfield sites to speed up work, while ensuring robust checks on flood risk, ecology and local impacts. We should also simplify and proportion the consultation process, so genuine local input remains, but without repetitive rounds that stall projects. 

This should go hand in hand with support for smaller builders and community-led housing, through local development orders and predictable milestones. In my town, a small affordable-housing block for key workers dragged on for nearly two years due to multiple reviews and duplicated consultations. Cutting unnecessary delays would bring costs down and make schemes viable, without compromising green space or energy standards. With sensible safeguards, these reforms can deliver more affordable, higher-quality homes for families here and nearby.

it's outrageous that from where I’m living in England, there’s a real squeeze between wanting more affordable homes and making sure what’s built is good quality and in sensible places. I don’t pretend to have all the answers, and I can see why people push different reform ideas. What follows are a few thoughts, not a single silver bullet, and I’m aware some would work in some places but not others.

Planning and speed of delivery
- I’d like to see the planning system simpler and faster, with clear, published deadlines and predictable outcomes. Too often decisions drag on, and that pushes up costs for builders and the eventual buyers or renters.
- On new schemes, I’d want a defined proportion of affordable homes, but with robust viability checks so that developers aren’t forced into schemes that collapse or become unviable later. The risk is a lot of paperwork without any real delivery.
- Small and local builders should be able to compete more fairly. In my town, a small builder wanted to convert a vacant factory site into around 15 homes, six of which would be affordable, but the process involved endless consultations, red tape and fees that made it hard to proceed. If there were quicker routes for smaller schemes, we might see more route-through to actual homes.
- Encourage development on brownfield sites first and give councils flexible tools to deal with land that’s currently unused. Green belt protections are important, but there should be a transparent mechanism to consider appropriate infill or renewal where local demand is high.

Using public land and funding more effectively
- Councils should have more freedom to make use of publicly owned land for affordable housing, with long-term leases to housing associations or community housing bodies. This could bring down build costs and speed things up if it’s done with proper borrowing rules and oversight.
- Right-to-buy receipts and other public funding should be used to back new affordable homes, not disappear into general budgets. Where possible, create a pipeline of sites and partnerships with local housing associations so that money is spent to deliver homes in those areas people actually need.
- Community-led approaches, like community land trusts, could help keep homes affordable for longer and give local people a real say in what gets built. In our area there’s potential for that if the council can provide the right support and a clear planning route.

Quality, standards and long-term stewardship
- It’s not just about building more homes; it’s about homes that stay affordable and maintainable. We need energy-efficient standards that don’t price people out of buying or renting, with clear guarantees for damp, mould and long-term maintenance.
- There have been worrying stories about new builds with defects or high maintenance costs. I’d want stronger post-completion oversight and a simple, enforceable maintenance model so residents aren’t left to pick up the tab for problems after they’ve moved in.
- Tenure mix matters. A balance of social rent, affordable rent, and shared ownership should be available, but not at a cost that traps families in expensive service charges or rising ground rents. A local person I know recently faced escalating charges on a shared ownership property, which makes budgeting fragile for people on modest incomes.

Local involvement and accountability
- Communities should have a real say in what gets built in their towns. Local planning panels or neighbourhood plans can help, as long as they operate fairly and transparently.
- I’d also want to see robust accountability for how schemes are managed after completion. If homes are going to be affordable, there should be a plan for long-term upkeep and for ensuring turnover to new households when the original residents’ circumstances change.

Bottom line
Overall, I think there isn’t a single reform that will fix everything. A package that combines quicker planning for small and mid-sized schemes, smarter use of public land, stable funding streams, strong but fair quality standards, and real local involvement seems sensible. But I worry about chasing speed at the cost of quality or inflating costs with green policies that aren’t properly adapted to the local economy. Any reforms should be piloted in a few areas first, with real monitoring and a clear guardrail to protect green spaces and long-term affordability.

If I had to pick one guiding principle, it would be: make it easier to build good-quality affordable homes on brownfield sites, with clear standards and long-term stewardship, and ensure communities have a real stake in the plan.

I’d prioritise regenerating towns through infill and converting vacant or long-term empty homes before any Green Belt release, to protect landscapes; support community land trusts, co-ops, self-build and modern methods of construction to boost affordable, good-quality homes quickly.

From our organisation’s perspective working across communities in England, the reforms that would most effectively increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes are those that lift data, accountability and delivery capability across the board. First, strengthen local data and monitoring: implement a live delivery dashboard that shows housing need assessments, permissions, starts, completions and the number of affordable homes delivered or promised on each site. In our experience, plans are approved on the basis of optimistic forecasts, then stall without transparent tracking. Second, tighten planning obligations and enforcement: make affordable housing contributions legally binding with clear delivery milestones, and apply penalties for missed targets or stalled sites. Independent viability checks should be routine, to prevent developers from using viability gaps to delay delivery. Third, improve developer accountability: publish quarterly performance data on Section 106 delivery and tie land value uplifts to timely provision of affordable homes. Clawback mechanisms should ensure funds or units are delivered if milestones slip. Fourth, increase council capacity: fund planning, enforcement and digital systems so conditions are monitored and delivered; enable quicker yet thorough decision-making without compromising quality. Finally, ensure funds are ring-fenced for delivery, with mechanisms to deliver on-site where possible and to phase affordable homes across attainable timelines. In a local site near us, 40 affordable homes promised in 2017 have only 12 delivered by 2024; better data and enforcement could have accelerated that outcome.

i strongly believe reforms should combine purpose-built Build-to-Rent with mixed-tenure housing, backed by affordability covenants and professional management, to boost long-term rental supply. In my area, rental stock often comes and goes, and when management is hands-off tenants bear the cost. A mature Build-to-Rent sector, with clear long-term leases, transparent maintenance standards and rent controls tied to local incomes, would provide stability.

Equally, we need rigorous upfront infrastructure planning: funded, phased delivery of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or even before housing to create sustainable, service-ready communities. That means planning conditions that secure these facilities before occupancy and investment in affordable homes early in the programme. I’ve seen schemes where new trains or GP access lag behind housing, which undermines quality of life.

Quality matters too: energy efficiency, robust on-site management, and enforceable covenants. It’s important the mix remains diverse so new areas aren’t monocultures or isolated dormitories. If reforms ensure long-term stewardship, accountability, and that facilities are in place as housing comes on, I would support them!

Yes, I strongly support reforms that improve local data, monitoring, developer accountability and funding to councils for planning, enforcement and delivery. In our area, a large development was approved with a promise of 40% affordable homes, but delivery has stretched over several years and the quality of the built homes leaves something to be desired. Public dashboards showing units completed, affordable units delivered, S106 obligations, and current planning milestones would help residents understand progress and push builders to meet their commitments.

Local councils need more capacity: funded planning teams, better enforcement resources, and a clear process to pause or revise permissions if delivery stalls. I would welcome ring-fenced funds to expand planning and monitoring capacity, plus stronger penalties for missed milestones and obligatory remedial work where standards fall short. Requiring monthly or quarterly updates from developers to the council, with accessible public reporting, would incentivise timely delivery and enable timely intervention.

In practice this means better data, clearer accountability, and real consequences for failing to deliver. That would give my neighbours and future generations the safer, decent, affordable homes our area needs.

Reforms should prioritise delivering more wheelchair‑accessible and adaptable homes, plus targeted older‑person, supported and student key‑worker accommodation. In practice this means designing new developments to universal design standards, with flexible layouts that can be reconfigured as needs change, and securing on-site support services where needed. Rural communities often lose out due to sparse stock and long commutes, while towns with universities need reliable, affordable housing for staff and students alike. In my area I have seen people with mobility issues wait years for suitable homes, and essential workers struggle to find close, affordable flats near work.

I’d also advocate pilots for rent caps or stabilization to improve affordability, but only if there is robust evidence on effects for supply and landlord participation. The risks—reduced investment, higher rents for non-capped units, or delay to maintenance—must be mitigated with time-limited schemes, exemptions for new build and social outcomes benchmarking. Tie affordability tools to deliverables: minimum new affordable units per development, maintained quality, and clear exit routes for investors.

Overall I'd support a mixed package: target‑led supply reforms to meet demographic and rural needs, paired with carefully evaluated affordability measures to prevent unintended consequences.

Living in England and watching energy prices rise, I think the reforms that will most effectively increase affordable, good-quality homes need to combine two strands: raising energy standards for new builds and funding genuine upgrades to the existing stock, alongside reform of how planning contributions are calculated and delivered. In my view this is not a trade-off; it’s a package where energy efficiency can actually reduce running costs for tenants and owners, making homes affordable to live in over the long term.

First, mandate higher energy standards for new builds and fund retrofits to cut bills. I welcome the direction of aiming for energy-efficient, low-carbon homes from day one. A fabric-first approach—good insulation, airtightness, efficient glazing, and low-carbon heating systems—will pay dividends for households already stretched by bills. The sooner we lock in higher standards, the less we’ll rely on subsidies to fix badly designed homes after people have moved in. In practical terms, I’d like to see: a clear, enforceable timeline for raising standards in all new-build homes, aligned with the government’s longer-term climate targets; better access to grants or low-interest loans for incremental costs so rent levels aren’t pushed up to cover them; and a nationwide retrofit fund that targets older stock, especially in the private rented sector where tenants often have little control over improvements. I’ve spoken to neighbours who rent and are continually worried about heating costs; a retrofit programme that capably reaches vulnerable households would relieve pressure on budgets and local services.

Second, reform Section 106, CIL and viability testing with transparency and enforceable obligations to secure on-site affordable homes and infrastructure funding. The current arrangements are opaque and sometimes fail to deliver the affordable housing we need locally. I’d like to see a reform path that guarantees delivery, with independent, publishable viability assessments and a clear line of sight from a scheme’s approvals through to funding for affordable homes and essential infrastructure.
- On-site affordable housing: local plans should set out minimum thresholds that are actually enforceable. If viability truly prohibits on-site affordable homes, there should be a credible, time-bound alternative (commuted sums) that is ring-fenced for affordable housing or infrastructure in the same locality, with strict caps and transparent costings.
- Transparency and accountability: viability assessments should be publicly available, with independent review where challenged. Planning decisions should come with a clear explanation if affordable housing is reduced or waived, and for every significant scheme there should be a detailed delivery plan showing how funding will be sourced and when.
- CIL and infrastructure funding: contributions should be index-linked and spent on locally identified priorities (schools, roads, GP capacity, flood defence, parks). The process should be streamlined to avoid unacceptable delays to development, but not at the expense of community needs.
- Fairness for small builders and community groups: ensure the reforms do not penalise smaller developers who can still deliver high-quality, affordable homes if supported with a simpler, faster process and appropriate viability benchmarks.

In my local area I’ve seen large developments proceed with optimistic viability statements that leave a relatively small slice of affordable housing, and projects sometimes stall while viability is reassessed. A more transparent approach would have given the community confidence and would have anchored investment in affordable homes and infrastructure sooner. I’m also aware of energy-efficiency expectations that aren’t fully baked into the planning process; better standards from the outset could reduce later retrofit costs and keep overall project economics from tipping unfavourably for renters.

Taken together, the reforms I’d like to see are: 1) legally binding energy standards for new homes, coupled with a robust fund for retrofits that protects tenants and reduces bills; 2) a revised, transparent, enforceable system for Section 106 and CIL that makes on-site affordable housing the default, with credible alternative funding only when viability is truly constrained, and with all viability evidence openly available; 3) a practical plan to ensure infrastructure (schools, transport, health facilities) keeps pace with housing growth; 4) transitional support for builders to adopt higher standards without crushing small developers or causing project delays.

Overall, I’m in favour of reforms that push energy efficiency and climate targets forward while guaranteeing that affordable, good-quality homes are genuinely delivered and maintained. The key is transparency, enforceability, and funding that vindicates the public investment by delivering homes that stay affordable for the people who live in them, for decades to come.

I welcome the opportunity to respond. In my view, the reforms that will most reliably increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes are those that two things at once: raise the standard of what is built, and make it easier and clearer for good schemes to progress from plan to completion. The three linked strands I’d prioritise are higher energy standards for new builds with funded retrofits, stronger local data and accountability for delivery, and carefully designed pilots for rent stability that guard against unintended harm while protecting households from unaffordable housing costs.

First, raising energy standards for new builds and funding retrofits across the board is essential. New homes should not be financed on the premise that rising energy bills will be someone else’s problem. I’d support rules that push new builds to be net‑zero ready and energy efficient from day one—for example fabric first targets, airtightness improvements, and on‑site low‑carbon heating or heat pumps with smart controls, plus opportunities for on‑site renewables. In practice this means mandating a clear, measurable minimum standard (e.g., EPC B or equivalent) by 2030, with programme funding to ensure builders can meet it without passing costs to tenants. Government and council schemes should fund retrofit works for existing rented homes, including cavity and solid wall insulation, boiler upgrades to heat pumps or other low‑carbon systems, and insulation improvements in blocks of flats where the benefit is greatest. These measures cut bills for tenants and reduce fuel poverty, while preventing the need for rapid, costly retrofit after tenants move in.

In our own area, energy costs for private tenants have risen sharply and there are examples of well‑conceived schemes stalled simply because the upfront retrofit work wasn’t funded or prioritised. If councils had dedicated retrofit funds and clear procurement routes, schemes could be delivered faster, improving comfort and affordability for tenants and reducing energy demand from new stock in the long term. I also welcome requirements that new developments include low‑carbon techniques and materials where feasible and that they provide data on actual energy use after occupancy, so performance can be assessed and improved on future projects.

Second, local data, monitoring and developer accountability are critical to ensure commitments are delivered. Too often, promises about affordable homes, delivery timelines, or infrastructure improvements do not translate into on‑the‑ground results because data are scattered or out of date and because delivery partners face weak consequences for delays. I’d back a robust, council‑led data system that tracks planning approvals, start on site dates, quarterly completion numbers, shares of affordable housing, and performance against energy and climate targets. Developers should publish delivery milestones and progress publicly, with penalties or clawbacks if milestones are missed without credible justification. This also means investing in planning and enforcement capacity at the local level—more skilled planners, better case management software, and clearer long‑lead timelines—so that viable schemes are not bottlenecked by capacity gaps.

From my experience, when a proposed 50‑home affordable scheme in our town was temporarily paused due to planning and network connection hurdles, the delay translated into higher costs and greater risk for both council and developers. If there had been stronger data visibility, early risk flags, and a dedicated delivery team, we could have kept the project moving and delivered homes sooner. I would therefore like to see councils funded to recruit and retain planning and enforcement staff, with incentives to coordinate cross‑department work (planning, building control, housing, energy efficiency) to keep schemes on track and to ensure promised affordable units are delivered.

Third, we should consider rent caps or stabilisation as pilots to improve affordability while evaluating impacts on supply and investment. It makes sense to test targeted, time‑limited stabilisation in high‑cost areas or in particular tenure mixes, with rigorous evaluation to understand effects on new development, landlord willingness to invest, and tenant outcomes. Any pilots should be accompanied by complementary measures—such as strong energy efficiency standards and retrofits, and clear conditions for continued investment—to avoid discouraging builders or landlords from taking on new stock. The aim would be to strike a balance: protecting households from sharp rent rises and sudden evictions, while preserving a viable investment environment so that developers and landlords continue to contribute to supply.

Other practical steps that would complement the reforms include: requiring affordable housing to be delivered on site as part of market developments where possible (or via well‑funded commuted sums where on‑site delivery isn’t feasible); prioritising brownfield land and small‑scale sites near transport links; and adopting modern methods of construction where they improve quality and speed without compromising durability or long‑term maintenance costs. Councils should also publish clear delivery standards and independent quality checks to ensure that new and retrofitted homes actually meet promised standards for energy efficiency, comfort, and safety.

In short, increasing supply while keeping homes affordable and high quality hinges on clear energy targets and retrofit funding, solid local data and strong delivery accountability, and carefully designed pilots that test rent stabilization without undermining investment. If these elements are joined up—funded, monitored and evaluated—I believe we can deliver more affordable homes that families can actually afford to live in, while helping us meet climate goals and reduce energy bills in the longer term.

Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes, with affordability covenants and professional management, could help secure long-term rental supply. However, as an older resident, keep rents predictable, ensure high-quality maintenance, and involve local residents to prevent displacement.

Living in a medium town in England, in my sixties, I see the housing challenge not just as bricks and mortar but as how a community stays affordable and livable. The most pressing issues on the ground aren’t only the number of new homes, but ensuring they are in the right places with good transport links, doctors, and schools. I’ve watched a local housing association project stall for almost two years because the planning process dragged, while a family on modest income was left waiting for a promised affordable unit that never materialised. At the same time, new builds that do go ahead sometimes lack proper insulation and energy efficiency, which makes running costs high and rents feel less affordable in the long term. I’m unsure which reforms would work best: faster planning decisions that still protect local input, stronger guarantees that affordable homes are built and maintained, and better standards for energy efficiency. Any reform should also invest in upgrading existing stock and local services so new homes do not strain what already exists.

Our area could benefit from reforms that treat housing delivery as part of a wider system, not a standalone target. I want more affordable, good-quality homes, but I’ve seen how new developments can strain local services if infrastructure and schools aren’t funded and planned in tandem. In practice, that means a more integrated, funded approach to planning where housing comes with the transport links, GP capacity, schools, and utilities that a growing community actually needs, and where the delivery is phased so that new homes aren’t left waiting for all the services to arrive later.

What I think would help most:

- Infrastructure-led planning with upfront funding: It should be standard that new housing comes with a credible plan and funding schedule for transport (roads, bus and rail improvements), health facilities, schools, and utilities before or alongside housing. In my town, a proposed estate has been stalled because the new primary school and expanded GP capacity aren’t funded yet. If infrastructure commitments were secured at the outset, developers, councils and NHS bodies could sequence building so that services are ready when families move in.

- Phased delivery tied to milestones: Create clear triggers that housing development can proceed only in steps that are matched by the delivery of the necessary services. This could be monitored through joint planning bodies with binding milestones. It would help prevent situations where blocks of homes are finished but fail to attract teachers, clinicians, or reliable public transport. If a phase is delayed, the next phase should be paused unless alternative service measures are put in place.

- Reform of funding mechanisms and local contributions: Developer contributions (Section 106-like agreements) and community infrastructure levies should be predictable, streamlined, and ring-fenced for local needs. The system should assure a fair mix of affordable homes and be explicit about where and how funds are spent, with a local chair or citizen oversight to maintain trust. In practice, this would mean a transparent formula for affordable housing that is delivered, maintained, and genuinely affordable to local people, not just a discount on market price.

- Support for serviced plots and brownfield-first delivery: Encourage and fund the provision of serviced plots on brownfield land first, so builders can start quickly and homes can be finished without long delays for utilities and connection works. This would also help reduce greenfield pressure and protect precious open spaces while still expanding supply.

- Strengthen support for smaller builders and community-led schemes: A more predictable pipeline and access to land, plus streamlined planning processes, would help regional small and mid-sized builders contribute to supply. Community-led and co-housing models can deliver high-quality, well-designed homes that fit local needs, provided they have suitable land, finance, and planning support.

- Quality, energy efficiency, and durable design: Reforms should incentivise high standards—good insulation, heat pumps or connection to low-carbon networks, durable materials, and accessible design. Establish design codes or performance standards for new communities to avoid later retrofit costs and energy waste.

- Local capacity and governance: Invest in planning departments and public-facing services to speed up decisions, with better data on land supply, housing needs, and service constraints. Regular progress reporting should be mandatory so residents can see how infrastructure and housing are aligning.

- Transit-oriented and job-holding developments: Align housing with local employment opportunities and good transport links. I’d like to see more mixed-use planning that keeps amenities within walking distance, reduces car dependency, and ensures new schools and clinics are not out of reach for the growing population.

- Safeguards and safeguards against fragmentation: There must be safeguards so that in the rush to build, environmental and community impacts aren’t ignored. Early community consultation, clear design expectations, and measurable environmental targets should be baked into every plan.

In short, I’m not against building more homes. I’m wary of insufficiently planned growth that outpaces services and depresses quality. A genuine reform package would make infrastructure an equal partner in housing policies: funded, phased, and embedded in the planning timetable so that every new community is service-ready, affordable, and capable of sustainably welcoming families without bulldozing existing neighbourhoods. If that balance can be achieved, I’d feel much more confident that reforms will deliver affordable, good-quality homes in my area rather than more churn and disappointment for long-standing residents.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. Our organisation represents local authorities, housing bodies and community groups across England, and we see a clear path to increasing the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes that are genuinely fit for purpose and well integrated with the services people rely on. We support reforms that stabilise rents in the longer term while protecting the willingness of private and affordable housing providers to invest, and we back infrastructure‑led delivery so that new communities are service‑ready from day one.

Key reforms we would prioritise are:

- Targeted, evidence‑led rent stabilization with pilots: We recognise the pressure on households from rising rents and the value of predictable costs. We support pilots of rent stabilization or caps in areas with acute affordability pressures, designed with clear evidence collection and independent evaluation. Cap design should be CPI or RPI plus a modest uplift, with an explicit exemption or staged uplift for properties that undertake high‑quality energy efficiency improvements or necessary decarbonisation works. Importantly, pilots should be time‑bound, geographically targeted, and accompanied by monitoring of tenancy stability, landlord exit rates, investment in maintenance, and the rate of new supply. The aim is to determine whether well‑designed, temporary caps can improve affordability without undermining long‑term investment in maintenance and new build.

- Funded, phased provision of infrastructure alongside housing: New communities must be ready to serve residents. We advocate for infrastructure plans that are funded in phases and formally linked to development milestones. This means early delivery of transport links, primary and secondary schools, GP capacity, utilities, digital connectivity and green space before or alongside housing. Where possible, use pooled budgets, developer contributions (CIL/S106) and public land releases to align housing with schools, medical facilities and sustainable transport. We welcome examples of “infrastructure‑first” blocks in garden towns and new settlements that deliver long‑term affordability as an outcome of well‑planned growth.

- Planning reforms and brownfield prioritisation with robust affordable housing targets: To accelerate supply, simplify planning processes for genuinely affordable and mission‑critical rental housing, particularly on brownfield sites. Accelerate planning permission with predictable timeframes and reduce viability disputes that stall delivery. Require a higher, clear minimum proportion of affordable housing in developments, with flexibility to reflect site constraints; ensure a mix of social rent, affordable rent, and discounted market rent where appropriate, and ensure new supply includes energy‑efficient, accessible homes designed for different life stages.

- Financing models that de‑risk and diversify supply: Support a stable pipeline by expanding models such as build‑to‑rent, community housing associations, cooperative housing, and value‑capture mechanisms that fund capital while keeping rents affordable. Support public sector land release and proactive land assembly to unlock sites for affordable housing. Consider guarantees or longer‑term revenue routes for lenders and investors to reduce refinancing risk and enable sustained maintenance budgets.

- Quality, energy efficiency and accessibility as mandatory standards: Make high standards the default for all new homes. Require fabric‑first energy performance, low‑carbon heating, durable finishes, and accessible design that can adapt to changing needs. Connect standards to rent levels where feasible, so households get long‑term savings on energy costs and maintenance.

- Tenant protections and landlord support to maintain supply: Provide incentives for landlords to stay in the market, such as long‑term leases with predictable rent reviews tied to inflation, grants or loans for energy efficiency upgrades, and clear, proportionate enforcement against poor practices. This helps reduce unnecessary landlord exit while preserving a route to affordable housing for those who private‑rent. 

- Strong data, monitoring and accountability: Establish a transparent, independent review mechanism to track affordable housing delivery, rent levels, investment signals, and the performance of pilots. Publish quarterly progress against targets and use lessons learned to adjust policy quickly.

In our area, affordability pressures persist, and the waiting lists for affordable housing remain substantial even where planning approvals are progressing. We have seen sites with strong development pipelines stall because essential services were not in place or because price pressures outpaced supply. A coordinated approach—where rents are stabilised in carefully chosen pilots, and every housing project comes with funded, predictable delivery of transport, schools and healthcare—would help ensure that new homes are not only built but are sustainable places to live.

We are ready to participate in pilots and provide robust local data to inform learning. By combining targeted affordability tools with infrastructure‑led delivery and clear planning reforms, we can increase considerably the number of truly affordable, high‑quality homes in our area while supporting stable investment and thriving communities.

From my years living in Scotland, I have seen how the lack of affordable, good‑quality homes affects families and, in particular, older neighbours who wish to downsize or stay in their communities but can’t find suitable options. I think reforms that streamline planning and decision timelines, while preserving essential environmental safeguards and robust community input, could unlock much-needed delivery without sacrificing quality or local character.

First, the planning process itself needs to be clearer, faster and more predictable. There should be statutory targets for decisions on straightforward housing schemes and clear, published timeframes for pre‑application discussions. A single, user‑friendly planning portal could replace the current maze of forms and delays, with pre‑application engagement that actually reduces downstream revision work. In practice, that means a 1‑stop process where applicants know the information required up front, and councils have enough resource to process applications promptly. Importantly, speed must not come at the expense of environmental safeguards; trees, flood risk, water quality and biodiversity must still be properly assessed, but those assessments should be proportionate and timely, not endless. Fast‑track routes could be offered for schemes that re‑use brownfield land, meet local affordable housing needs and demonstrate robust infrastructure plans, with independent checks to prevent corner‑cutting.

Second, there should be careful reform of zoning and decision timelines that rewards delivery while protecting places. Local plans should be kept up to date, and there should be a stronger emphasis on brownfield redevelopment before greenfield release. Decision timelines could be streamlined by reducing duplication between agencies and councils and by providing a clear mechanism for early agreement on essential infrastructure (road access, drainage, schools, GP capacity). Where affordable housing is included, the plan should set out deliverability milestones that are legally binding, with consequences if milestones are missed. This would reduce developer uncertainty and give communities confidence that promised homes will be built.

Third, we must hard‑wire environmental safeguards into any speedier system. I’m not asking for weaker protection; I’m asking for smarter sequencing. Environmental impact and climate resilience checks should be front‑loaded and outcome‑focused, not used to stall good schemes. Sufficient flood risk management, ecological surveys, and climate adaptation measures must be part of the standard application, with clear criteria for mitigation and monitoring. The goal is to avoid later retrofits that cost councils and residents more and delay finished homes.

Fourth, local data, monitoring and accountability are essential. Councils should maintain an up‑to‑date housing need and supply register, with public dashboards showing how many affordable homes are in the pipeline, how many have started on site, and how many meet agreed delivery milestones. Developers should report progress at set intervals, and there should be transparent reporting on any delays, with swift remedies. I know from personal experience that our area’s housing lists can be out of date, which leads to mismatches between what’s planned and what families actually need. A robust data framework would help ensure sites with planning approvals actually deliver the promised affordable units.

Fifth, funding and capacity for planning and enforcement must be strengthened. Councils should receive ring‑fenced funding to expand planning teams, apply digital tools, and recruit enforcement staff so that projects don’t stall while work waits for scarce planners. In several towns I’m aware of, backlog and limited enforcement capacity allow developers to miss milestones with little consequence; this must change. A credible system would include performance bonds or similar protections, so where a project stalls, councils or a third party can step in to maintain progress and protect public interest.

Sixth, delivery capacity should be boosted through governance models that enable delivery partners to work with communities. We should encourage more community land trusts, cooperative housing and partnerships with housing associations to bring projects to completion more quickly and at lower cost. Allowing landowners and councils to jointly prepare sites with clear affordability requirements can help ensure that the homes built truly meet local need and can be kept affordable over time.

Seventh, infrastructure and place quality matter as much as the number of homes. Reforms should require upfront agreements on essential infrastructure and services, and provide funding to unlock sites where infrastructure constraints are a barrier to delivering homes. That way, developers aren’t faced with inescapable extra costs after planning consent and communities won’t endure years of hold‑ups while roads, drains or schools lag behind.

In summary, I support reforms that make the planning system faster, more predictable and better financed, but with strong, independent checks that keep environmental protections and local safeguards intact. If we implement streamlined decision‑making, better data and accountability, and expanded council capacity to plan and enforce, we can bring forward more affordable, good‑quality homes that meet real local need without compromising the places we love.

We need reforms like better local data, stricter enforcement and funded planning capacity, plus a clear focus on regeneration, infill and converting vacant or long-term empty homes before releasing greenfield sites to protect landscapes.

From where I live in England, the big challenge isn’t only about building more houses, but making sure they’re actually affordable and well-sited for everyday life. I’ve seen rents rise in my town, with two-bedroom flats now out of reach for many graduates starting out. In my view, reforms should prioritise practical delivery: faster planning decisions, clearer routes for brownfield development, and better funding to bring vacant blocks back into use without displacing neighbours. Yet even with more supply, quality matters just as much as quantity—long-lasting repairs, insulation, and safe running costs should be part of any package. My street has a block with damp issues and delayed upgrades, and that sort of deterioration will push up costs for households that can least afford it. So alongside new builds, I’d like to see incentives for energy efficiency and longer-term maintenance funds, plus renter protections during regeneration. The balance between growth and preserving local character is delicate, and I’m not sure one reform on its own will fix it.

I disagree with moves to unlock more greenfield land or dilute Green Belt protections as a quick fix for affordable housing. In my area there are plenty of brownfield and town-centre opportunities that would deliver good-quality homes far faster if we prioritised regeneration, infill and the conversion of vacant buildings and long-term empty homes over any greenfield release. A derelict factory on our High Street has been idle for years; converting it into affordable flats would add housing capacity now, with lower service and infrastructure costs than a new build on greenfield land. 

Equally, reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing must be about enforceable obligations and real transparency, not loopholes. I’ve seen cases where viability arguments effectively erase on-site affordable housing or leave funds unspent for years. We need robust, publishable viability assessments, time‑bound delivery of affordable units, and mandatory on-site provision where viable, with clear penalties if not delivered. CIL funds must be ring-fenced for local infrastructure and affordable housing, not absorbed into general budgets. 

If reforms are to work, they should incentivise regeneration first, with tight governance and predictable outcomes, so landscapes, biodiversity and local services are protected while delivering affordable homes more quickly on appropriate sites.

I support reform of Section 106, CIL and viability testing, with greater transparency and enforceable obligations to secure on-site affordable homes and infrastructure funding. In our area, too many schemes promise affordable homes at planning stage but the viability assessments later erode that commitment. Publishing the assumptions behind viability tests—including build costs, market values and allowances for affordable units—would help the public understand decisions. Requiring on-site delivery of affordable homes as a condition of occupation, or clear staged triggers, would prevent schemes from backtracking after consent. CIL funding should be more tightly linked to local infrastructure needs—roads, school places, GP capacity, green spaces—and be ring-fenced or independently audited. I’d like to see independent viability audits and penalties for non-compliance, so developers cannot simply claim financial overviews to avoid delivery. If these reforms are implemented, we will see more affordable, good-quality homes built in suitable locations without harming town centres or existing communities.

From where I live in England, affordable, good-quality homes are hampered not just by price but by a slow, uncertain pipeline of sites that local SME builders can actually bid for. Reforms that would have the biggest impact, in my view, centre on finance, procurement access and small-sites planning support. A targeted finance and guarantees package for SME and local builders—paired with a clearer, faster procurement route in which councils set aside a share of affordable- housin contracts for local firms—would help diversify supply and keep build costs closer to reality for first-timee buyrrs and renters. The small-sites policy should be accelerated: releasing, with clear feasibility and stewardship rules, smaller brownfield plots and surplus council land and providing pre-application planning advice to reduce delay and cost for small builders to land a project. In my area, a local SME faced a months-long funding hurdle and a lengthy planning process that stopped a 12-home scheme from progressing; improved access to patientt finance and strramlined approvals could have unlocked that supply. On licensing, enforcement and quality standards, I’m wary of costs that coul pus small landlords out. I’d support proportionate, well-targeted checks, with exemptions for landlords who maintain high standards and participate in tenancy support schemes. Longer tenancies can be encouraged but must be paired with protections for landlords’ viability, perhap via tax/guarantee options or rent-uptake support for troubled properties. Overall, a measured blend of SME-focused finance, planning simplification and balanced regulation would bestt lift supply without sacrificing quality.

I live in England and I welcome reforms to increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes. I think combining community land trusts, housing co-operatives, self-build, and modern methods of construction can deliver new homes quickly while keeping them genuinely affordable and well-built. In our area, a community land trust model could steward a small cluster of affordable homes on a former council site, with long-term affordability through a shared equity model. Co-ops offer tenancy security and democratically run estates, which helps communities feel invested.

I also believe releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift through levies could fund affordable homes and local infrastructure. Where a brownfield site sits idle, public land should be offered at transparent, affordable rates to affordable housing developers; the uplift from planning gains should be ring-fenced for housing and local infrastructure such as roads, schools, and flood defenses.

A practical example from local work: a small-scale self-build cooperative could build five to ten low-energy homes in phases, with modern methods of construction cutting site time and waste. We must set clear delivery standards and ensure access to finance and skill training.

Living in England and watching housing costs in my area rise faster than wages, I think the biggest gains come from reforms that empower small and local builders to bring forward diverse, community-sized schemes, alongside growing a stable long‑term rental sector that stays affordable. A package that combines targeted finance, smarter procurement, and planning support for SME builders with a strong Build‑to‑Rent/ mixed‑tenure approach would work best in practice, but it has to be designed with safeguards to avoid price inflation and poor quality.

Finance and procurement for SMEs is where I see real bottlenecks. Public money is often tied to large, national developers, while local builders who know the plots and the area face higher interest rates, stricter collateral requirements and longer, more opaque decision timelines. A practical reform would be a government‑backed SME development fund or loan guarantees specifically for small sites (say up to 20–30 units). Local authorities could partner with niche lenders to deliver small, low‑risk loans in an initial phase, with a clear schedule to scale up. This would translate into more diversified supply across towns and suburbs, not just in expensive city centres. In my area, a 12‑unit brownfield site near the station has stalled because the loan term and risk assessment make it uneconomic for a small builder; a targeted guarantee or a starter equity facility would unlock it and create genuinely affordable homes locally.

Procurement access needs to be more SME‑friendly. Public housing programmes should reserve a portion of small‑site contracts for SME builders and local consortia, with streamlined pre‑qualification and shorter tender windows. We could see Frameworks that allow “local lots” to be bid in a simple, price‑weighted route, with clear criteria on quality and local supply chains. A faster, more predictable procurement timetable—complete with a single-point pre‑application advice service and planning performance agreements—would reduce delays and allow SMEs to plan capital and employ local tradespeople, apprenticeships included.

The small‑sites policy and planning support must be more proactive. Many councils still treat small sites as marginal and struggle with viability testing that hurts smaller schemes. I’d like to see a national small‑sites policy that designates certain plots (up to around 0.5–1 hectare, 5–30 units) for SME development, with guaranteed quick planning decisions (for example, a 8–12 week determination window) and simplified viability testing that protects small builders from being priced out by hedged assumptions. Release of council land and community assets for small, well designed developments—particularly on brownfield sites near good transport links—would also help. Support for custom‑build and self‑build on small plots should be integrated, with planning guidance that makes this workable rather than a novelty.

On Build‑to‑Rent and mixed tenure, I’m supportive, but it must deliver long‑term affordability and quality. Purpose‑built rental can stabilise rents and improve management standards if it’s properly regulated. The government could encourage BTR by offering longer planning horizons and density allowances tied to a required share of genuinely affordable units within each scheme. Affordability covenants—secured for decades, ideally aligned with local income levels—should be mandatory, not optional, and should be backed by professional, on‑site property management to maintain standards and energy efficiency. A mix of rented, shared ownership, and discount market rent in BTR developments would help new entrants into the housing ladder while protecting the longevity of the stock.

In practice, this combination would require careful monitoring and local accountability. I’d want to see a local housing supply charter with clear targets for SME‑led small‑site delivery alongside BTR with covenants, plus transparent reporting on tenant satisfaction, energy performance, and long‑term stewardship. The goal isn’t big‑brand speculation but steady, incremental growth of well‑designed, affordable homes that stay affordable and well managed for the long term. If done with proper safeguards and granularity—local ladders, local jobs, and high quality standards—it could finally push up the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in areas like mine.

As an organisation delivering and campaigning for affordable, good-quality homes in England, we disagree with proposals that push housing supply without binding, funded infrastructure and services to accompany it. Reforms must mandate phased provision of transport networks, schools capacity, healthcare access and essential utilities alongside new homes, with upfront or ring-fenced funding. Otherwise new developments become car-dependent, strain local NHS and schools, and fail the affordability test once prices rise to cover extra trips and delays.

We also urge a robust emphasis on housing that meets actual needs: more wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes; additional older-person and supported housing; and student or key-worker homes in rural and culturally diverse areas. These must be delivered as part of the same phased plans, with planning rules requiring inclusive design and tenure mix to reflect local demographics.

In our area, a recent plan for 600 homes would overwhelm the nearest GP practice and the few bus routes serving the village. A service-ready, infrastructure-backed approach would deliver sustainable, affordable homes that communities can genuinely sustain.

I welcome the reforms proposed to increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. As someone living in England and watching local housing costs rise, I believe a mixed approach will deliver faster and more sustainable results than any one policy alone. In particular, I think community-led models, smarter use of public land, and sensible affordability measures should sit at the heart of reform.

First, we should back community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, self‑build groups and modern methods of construction. CLTs and housing co‑operatives keep homes affordable for the long term because land is held for the community and rents or charges are set with local need in mind. They also give residents real influence over design and day‑to‑day management, which helps ensure new homes fit the area rather than becoming speculative assets. There are already successful CLT and cooperative projects in several parts of England delivering affordable homes that meet high design and energy standards. In addition, self‑build groups, supported by MMC—such as modular timber-frame or cross‑laminated timber construction—can shorten build times, improve energy efficiency, and reduce waste. If councils earmark land for these models, provide access to finance through local authority loans at reasonable rates, and offer streamlined planning processes (for pre‑approved MMC designs that meet local codes), we can get much-needed homes on the ground quickly. Locally, there is real interest among nurses, teachers and shop workers to participate in community-led schemes, which would help retain key workers and sustain local services.

Second, release surplus public land and capture planning uplift to fund affordable homes and local infrastructure. Councils hold land that often sits idle, while the demand for affordable housing and health, education and transport infrastructure grows. Releasing suitable public land for genuinely affordable housing—coupled with mechanisms to capture uplift from planning gains—could fund new homes and the facilities families rely on. Using planning obligations and taxes or levies to return a portion of uplift to local housing, schools and GP capacity would align land value with community needs. I’d like to see pilots in a few districts to test this approach, with clear metrics on homes delivered, unit sizes, and the infrastructure that gets funded. The aim should be transparent, accountable use of receipts so residents can see the direct benefits in their streets and schools.

Third, consider rent caps or stabilisation to improve affordability while evaluating risks to supply, investment and landlord exit effects via pilots and evidence. A carefully designed, time-limited pilot could help us understand how caps or stabilisation would affect rents in practice, tenant security and the willingness of landlords to maintain and invest in their properties. Any scheme must protect landlords’ legitimate costs and avoid discouraging new investment or driving good landlords from the market. I would support pilots that combine rent stability with longer secure tenancies, while maintaining a pathway to high-quality, well‑managed rental housing. The aim should be to reduce pressure on households who are paying a large share of income on rent, without inadvertently shrinking the number of homes available to rent.

To make these reforms work, it will be vital for national and local bodies to collaborate on delivery. Identify land suitable for community land trusts, co‑ops and MMC; set up funding streams to support self‑build housing; streamline procurement for MMC projects; and ensure planning rules incentivise affordable homes rather than delay them. Strong governance, transparency, and ongoing community involvement will be essential. If delivered well, these reforms could increase supply quickly, raise quality, and keep homes affordable for long‑term residents, including families and older neighbours who want to remain in the places they know. I’m hopeful that, with careful piloting and robust evaluation, we can build a fairer, more resilient housing system for our area.

i really think i strongly support reforms that boost affordable, good-quality homes by expanding purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure developments with affordability covenants and professional management. These approaches deliver long-term, secure rental homes while maintaining quality and good management. In my area, recently completed BTR blocks with on-site teams have been well-run, with quick repairs and predictable rents that don’t spike year on year. When schemes include affordability covenants for 10-20 years and mix rented and shared-ownership or discounted market rent units, families can plan and stay in their communities.

Policy levers: streamline planning for BTR, provide tax incentives or density bonuses for BTR, require a minimum proportion of genuinely affordable homes within schemes, and mandate professional management with transparent service charges and clear handling of repairs. Also ensure energy efficiency and accessible design.

Conclusion: by making Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes a central pillar, we can grow long-term rental supply without compromising quality, which is essential for stability and local economy!

Thank you for giving residents a chance to share views on how we can increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes in Wales. I’m responding as an individual living in Wales, in the 35-44 age bracket, and I strongly support reforms that speed up delivery while keeping safeguards in place. The housing shortage has real, tangible impacts on families here, including rising rents and longer waits for genuinely affordable homes. With the right mix of reform, we can cut red tape without letting standards slip.

First, simplifying and streamlining planning, zoning and decision timelines is crucial, as long as environmental safeguards are retained. In my experience, the delay between outline permission and actual construction can stall sites that would otherwise deliver affordable units. A clear, capped decision timetable would help developers plan and lenders to commit without holding back. This should be supported by a one-stop, digitally integrated planning system that speeds up routine approvals while allowing for proper scrutiny where needed. Importantly, we should accelerate genuine brownfield redevelopment, with clear expectations for affordable provision attached to permission and a faster route for reserved matters when the site already meets environmental and design standards.

Second, local data, monitoring, and accountability must rise to meet the scale of the challenge. Councils should have robust, publicly available dashboards showing current housing supply, the pipeline for affordable homes, and delivery against commitments. Developers should be required to report quarterly on the number of affordable homes delivered, with penalties for non-delivery or delays beyond agreed milestones. This is not about punishment for councils or developers alone, but about giving communities clear sight of progress and focusing resources where they’re needed. To deliver, councils also need adequate capacity: targeted funding to expand planning departments, invest in digital case-management tools, and recruit planning officers who can process complex sites efficiently without compromising quality.

Third, there should be a clear plan to improve enforcement and delivery capacity at the local level. Too many promised schemes stall because of slow enforcement of planning conditions or a lack of specialist staff to monitor delivery. Ring-fenced funding and performance benchmarks for planning, enforcement, and delivery teams can help ensure commitments translate into completed homes. This could also include independent verification of completed affordable units before release of final payments, limiting the risk that a project claims success without delivering.

On affordability more broadly, I welcome pilots around rent caps or stabilization to test whether tighter rents in high-demand areas can improve living standards without deterring investment or constraining new supply. It’s important these pilots are evidence-based and time-limited, with clear metrics on impact to supply, investment signals, and landlord willingness to exit or invest long-term. For example, if a tenant’s rent stabilisation reduces displacement and keeps families in their communities, that’s a public good. But we must monitor unintended consequences: reduced returns could slow new-build and maintenance, or push landlords to convert properties to other uses. Pilots should be designed with input from tenants, landlords, and lenders, and include robust exit strategies and support for small landlords who want to continue providing housing.

To illustrate with local experience, when our council rolled out a digital planning portal and introduced a local pre-application meeting that brought consultees together early, decisions moved faster and developers were more confident about delivering affordable units on-site or through secured agreements. Conversely, sites that lack clear timing or delivery obligations often sit idle for years. These examples show how the right processes can convert planning approvals into actual homes.

In summary, I believe the most effective reforms combine speed with accountability and prudence. Streamlining planning timelines and decisions, backed by accessible local data and adequate council capacity, will accelerate delivery. Pair that with measured pilots on rent stabilization, designed to protect tenants while preserving investment incentives, and with robust monitoring of outcomes, and we can make tangible progress toward affordable, good-quality homes across Wales.

I’d urge policymakers to design reforms in close consultation with local authorities, housing associations, landlords, and residents like me. The goal should be more homes coming online on predictable timetables, with quality and sustainability safeguarded for communities now and in the future.

Releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift are pragmatic routes to boost affordable, good-quality homes in our area. Local councils hold sites that have sat idle for years—old school sites, airfields, or surplus council housing land. Transferring these to housing associations and developers under clear conditions (like mandatory affordable quotas and high energy standards) would reduce land costs and accelerate delivery. In my town there is a former hospital site and a police depot near the town centre; if released for mixed-tenure housing with 40-60% affordable homes, we could ease pressure on the private market while supporting older residents who want to downsize locally. 

Capturing planning uplift through levies or taxes—such as a land-value uplift levy when planning permission increases value or through CIL/S106 funding—should be ring-fenced to affordable homes and local infrastructure (schools, GP surgeries, streets). This ensures gains are invested locally rather than absorbed by developers. The reforms must be straightforward, with simple eligibility rules, quick decision times, and robust quality requirements (space, accessibility, energy efficiency). If done well, these reforms will deliver decent homes sooner and keep communities intact.

Agree. I believe reforms to release surplus public land and to capture planning uplift will help bring down land costs and fund affordable homes and local infrastructure. In my area, there are council-owned sites that have been unused for years and brownfield land that could support new homes without eating into green spaces. If the planning uplift from development is recycled through dedicated levies or taxes for affordable housing, we could reduce the upfront cost of schemes and speed up delivery. A clear ring-fence would be essential so the funds go to genuinely affordable homes rather than road repairs alone.

I also back major public investment in council and housing association building programmes to deliver long‑term social rented homes for low‑income households. Waiting lists in our borough are long and many families live in overcrowded or unsuitable housing. Government backing for modern, energy-efficient social rented homes would stabilise households, cut energy costs, and free up private-rented stock for others. I’d like to see speedier planning approvals and strong local targets to ensure these homes become a reality in the next five to ten years.

i strongly believe from where I sit in England, housing policy cannot be separated from the services that make a place livable. A reform that would help most is funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or even before new homes, so communities are ready to thrive rather than waiting years for basic services. Without that, cheaper housing quickly becomes a problem of isolation and burden on existing facilities.

Practical steps I’d back include: (1) infrastructure-linked phasing agreements that tie completions to field-ready schools, GP capacity and bus/rail improvements; (2) expanding purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes with affordable covenants and professional management to sustain a stable, long-term rental supply; (3) cautious pilots of rent caps or stabilisation to improve affordability, but only with robust monitoring and evidence on impacts to investment and landlord exit; (4) streamlined planning for small sites and brownfield redevelopment to accelerate delivery while maintaining high design and energy standards; (5) local plans that align housing with local employment and healthcare capacity.

In my area I’ve seen a proposed estate stall when schools couldn’t expand in time, while elsewhere Build-to-Rent projects have delivered better-maintained blocks with longer-tenure stewardship. I support reforms that couple housing with serviced infrastructure and careful affordability protections, provided we pilot and evaluate the effects to avoid reducing overall supply.

I agree: mandating higher energy standards and funding retrofits will cut bills and meet targets; stronger licensing and longer tenancies with protections for small landlords; and more accessible, adaptable homes for older people, wheelchair users, students and key workers, tailored to local needs.

Releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift via levies to fund affordable housing and local infrastructure could be a meaningful way to boost supply, but it must be done carefully. As a young person renting in a city centre, I know how quickly land costs feed into rents and property prices. If the uplift from development is captured (via CIL or Section 106 contributions) to fund genuinely affordable homes and essential local services, it could help deliver transport links, schools and GP capacity alongside new housing rather than letting costs spiral. 

However, the affordable homes must be genuinely affordable for local young people—social or affordable rents, with long-term tenure protections. Clear quotas, robust design standards, and protection of remaining green space are essential. The process must be transparent, with communities involved in site selection and in how uplift revenue is spent. 

I’m cautious about potential downsides: levy rates that raise development costs could slow schemes or push prices up elsewhere. I’d want pilots with rigorous evaluation on the number and permanence of affordable homes delivered, and on whether local infrastructure actually improves. If deployed with strong safeguards, it could help, but it needs careful, accountable delivery.

I disagree that generic planning reforms alone will boost supply; we need measures prioritising wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes for older people, plus supported and student key‑worker housing tailored to rural and cultural needs, with proper funding and simpler approvals.

As an organisation delivering housing support in England, I welcome the goal of increasing affordable, good‑quality homes but I’m cautious about whether the proposed reforms alone will deliver in practice. In our area, the biggest blockers aren’t simply the number of permissions, but the cost and pace of building, the availability of skilled trades, and the ability to retrofit existing stock to modern standards.

For example, a recent project to upgrade a block of council flats built in the 1980s required six months just to secure compliant electrical works because of shortages and complex procurement routes. The upgrades improved warmth and lower bills, but the upfront capital and delays erased some savings and dampened demand from tenants.

Therefore, reforms should pair supply with capital for energy efficiency retrofits, plus clearer, faster planning routes for brownfield sites and repurposed buildings. Supporting local builders with contracts, reducing red tape in procurement, and guaranteeing long-term maintenance funding would help keep all homes good‑value and safe. We also need accessibility standards and climate resilience built into every scheme to protect against cost‑of‑living shocks.

In short, a holistic package that links building, retrofit, maintenance, and local capacity would be more effective than supply‑only changes.

absolutely i live in England and have seen more and more of our housing stock fall into disrepair or stay empty while waiting lists grow longer. As an older person, I’m worried that simply piling in more homes without insisting on standards and long-term affordability will do little to help those who need decent, stable places to live. I don’t think the answer lies in chasing supply numbers alone; we need reform that protects tenants, supports small landlords, and unlocks community‑led approaches that can deliver real affordable quality much faster.

First, stronger licensing, enforcement and minimum quality standards are essential, but they must be designed so they don’t push small landlords away or deter investment in needed housing. If licensing is too costly or has bureaucratic loopholes, some decent landlords will withdraw, reducing supply just when we need it most. I’d like to see a clear, easily understood national framework for private rented licensing with reasonable fees and realistic penalties for serious penalties or repeated failures. Landlords should be required to meet safety and energy efficiency standards (gas/electrical safety, damp and mould remediation, and at least a credible EPC). Councils need properly funded enforcement teams that can act quickly when problems arise, not rely on overstretched volunteers or delayed prosecutions. A visible, consistent standard would help tenants know where they stand and give landlords a fair playing field.

Second, I welcome the move towards longer tenancies, provided they come with protections against unfair rent increases and eviction practices. Stability matters especially for older residents who fear moving house at the wrong time. But longer tenancies must be paired with caps on excessive rent hikes, and options for tenants to transfer improvements or benefit from energy‑efficiency upgrades without losing security. I’d favour tenancy support services through local authorities to help tenants understand their rights and help landlords manage repairs, so tenancies aren’t ended simply because maintenance costs rise.

Third, we must recognise the fragility of many small landlords. If the regime becomes too punitive or too expensive, some owners will exit, which worsens shortages. I’d advocate targeted support for small landlords to upgrade properties to meet standards, including grants or low‑interest loans for energy improvements, damp remediation, and fire safety upgrades. Fees and red‑tape should be proportionate to property size and risk, not one‑size‑fits‑all. It’s not about shielding every landlord but about ensuring a viable path to bringing substandard homes up to scratch without depriving local families of places to live.

Beyond regulation, I think the most promising reforms are those that bring in community‑led models: community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, self‑build projects, and modern methods of construction (MMC). In our area there are underused parcels that could accommodate modest, energy‑efficient homes if land is held in trust for the community and projects are not buried under planning delays. CLTs and co‑ops can maintain long‑term affordability because the land is held separately from the homes, so resale prices stay within reach for successive generations. Self‑build on smaller plots can help older residents who want to downsize but stay in the same neighbourhood, while MMC (factory‑built or modular homes) can speed up delivery, reduce waste and improve quality control.

To make this work, government needs to back planning fast‑tracking for community‑led schemes, provide capital for land acquisition and construction, and create partnerships with councils to unlock brownfield sites. Local pilots that combine CLTs with modern construction techniques could deliver affordable homes much quicker than traditional building, without sacrificing quality. Investment in infrastructure around these sites—public transport links, schools, GP capacity—will also pay off in the long run by supporting sustainable communities.

In short, I’d oppose reforms that chase higher numbers of dwellings at the expense of safety, upkeep and affordability for tenants.
