Proximity to GP services, shops, and decent public transport is crucial; otherwise, even a “well-built” home can become a financial and social burden for someone who cannot get out easily in winter. Long-term maintenance sums must accompany the build programmes, so these are not short-lived bursts of construction but sustainable investments that keep communities safe and fit for purpose for decades.

To enable this, funding needs to be consistent and predictable. That means central government providing ring-fenced capital, with councils allowed to borrow prudently against predictable revenue streams from social rents, to deliver not just one-off schemes but a pipeline of homes over 10–15 years. The goal should be to crowd in housing associations and private sector partners only where it adds value, while preserving the social mission and ensuring value for money through strong procurement that prioritises quality and safety over cheapest price.

Second, planning reform should accelerate delivery while protecting the environment and public interest. Streamlining planning, zoning and decision timelines is essential to reduce the endless delays that push up costs and stall projects. Practical targets would help: faster pre-application engagement, with clear timelines for responses; decisions on straightforward schemes within a tight window; and a presumption in favour of affordable housing on suitable brownfield sites, subject to meeting essential safeguards. The aim is to reduce developer uncertainty and keep projects moving so communities do not endure years of waiting while housing pressures mount.

That said, speed must not come at the expense of safety or balance. I want to see robust environmental safeguards: biodiversity net gain, flood risk assessments, climate resilience, and energy efficiency standards embedded in all schemes. Community involvement should be real and meaningful, not a box-ticking exercise. Where local objections are valid, the planning system should provide clear, transparent reasons and reasonable compromises—for example, ensuring that new developments fit with local character, provide adequate parking or public transport links, and avoid over-concentration of blocks in a single street.

In practice, a mixed approach would work well: build on brownfield sites, use surplus or underused public land, and mix tenures on developments to support social stability. A genuine 25–40% social or affordable rent component on qualifying sites could ensure supply goes to those most in need, with the remainder allocated at affordable levels. Importantly, councils must have the capacity to manage these homes long term, including repairs, energy upgrades, and tenancy support, so the benefits endure and do not dissipate through neglect.

In summary, I support a dual approach: substantial, publicly funded programmes of high-quality, energy-efficient social housing, and a planning system that is faster but never at the expense of safety, inclusivity, and environmental responsibility. If implemented well, these reforms could noticeably reduce waiting lists, stabilise communities, protect vulnerable households from escalating private rents, and ease pressure on the NHS and social services by reducing housing insecurity and fuel poverty. Please keep communities informed, protect green and flood-prone areas, and ensure there is genuine accountability for how funds are spent and homes are maintained long into the future.

From where I live in England, private rents range from well-kept homes to properties that suffer damp, mould, or slow repairs. Reforms need to be pragmatic and balanced: I want higher standards without pushing small landlords out of the market. First, strengthen licensing and enforcement by extending selective licensing to areas with high private-rented turnover and conducting regular inspections focused on safety, damp and fire risk; require mandatory electrical safety checks and working alarms in every home. Second, raise minimum quality standards with a clear baseline for repairs and energy efficiency, plus practical support for landlords to meet it (grant funds or interest-free loans for safety upgrades and insulation rather than punitive penalties alone). Third, promote longer tenancies while protecting small landlords: allow 3- to 5-year tenancies with transparent, fair rent reviews and provide incentives for landlords who offer stability (tax relief or licensing-fee reductions). Finally, boost supply: speed planning for conversions of underused buildings, back Build-to-Rent and ensure affordable-housing quotas on new schemes, with local advisory support for small landlords navigating upgrades. In my experience, stable, well-regulated tenancies combined with targeted upgrades would improve living conditions and gradually increase affordable supply.

I strongly support reforms that will boost the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. A mix of community‑led models and clearer funding/viability rules is the quickest route to deliver lasting benefits. 

Community land trusts and housing co‑operatives can lock land into local ownership and maintain affordability over the long term. In our area, a local CLT secured a small brownfield site and delivered 12 affordable homes with community space and solar panels. A nearby village housing co‑op converted a disused school into 8 energy‑efficient homes, with residents helping to manage and maintain the scheme. Self‑build schemes and modern methods of construction can speed delivery and raise quality—factory‑built modular homes have shown fast delivery and improved insulation, which reduces bills for residents. 

On the funding side, reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing with greater transparency and enforceable obligations is essential. We need clear requirements for on‑site affordable homes, or robust, verifiable off‑site contributions, with viability assessments published and scrutinised. Ring‑fencing funds for affordable housing and essential infrastructure will help communities feel the benefits are real and lasting.

I disagree that the reforms as framed will reliably increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in Wales. While higher energy standards for new builds align with climate targets, they push up construction costs and can push rents higher, which worsens affordability in practice. Funding retrofits is important, but if delivery of those funds slows or becomes a bottleneck, it won’t help households who still can’t access decent homes. 

Reforms to Section 106, CIL and viability testing, even with more transparency, risk developers negotiating away affordable obligations or delaying schemes while tests are resolved. In my area a medium‑sized site has been stalled for months over viability discussions, with little certainty that any affordable homes will materialise. 

Requiring funded, phased provision of transport, schools and healthcare before housing sounds sensible, but in practice it slows projects and dampens supply, especially where local authorities already struggle to deliver services. A more effective package would prioritise faster, predictable planning decisions, sensible viability thresholds, and ring‑fenced, timely funding for infrastructure and retrofit programs that improve bills without delaying the new homes supply.
Not sure which reforms work best here; planning delays and costs seem key, but we need local input and clear standards to keep quality.

Across our housing programmes in England, the route to more affordable, good-quality homes lies in reforms that treat energy efficiency as a core capability, not an optional extra. Mandating higher energy standards for new builds and financing retrofit of existing stock will stabilise costs for tenants and create clearer incentives for developers.

For new builds, we support a fabric-first, near-zero carbon standard with airtightness, high insulation, efficient sizing of heating systems, and heat-pump readiness, with on-site renewables where viable. To avoid pricing out builders, provide transitional funding, tax relief, and a streamlined planning pathway so higher standards don’t slow delivery.

For existing homes, scale retrofit funding through a mix of central grants, public-backed loans, and local authority programmes, prioritising social housing and private rented sector stock. Clear timelines (e.g., retrofitting the bulk of social housing within 5 years, the wider private stock within 7–10 years) and simple application processes will help. Our pilots show energy bills dropping by around 20–30% after insulation and efficient heating—benefits that make more affordable homes financially viable for households.

Delivery must be joined up with planning policy, workforce training, and targeted developer contributions to fund efficiency, plus independent reporting to monitor savings and rent impacts. Taken together, these reforms can unlock more affordable homes while delivering climate targets and avoiding disproportionate costs for tenants and landlords.

I strongly disagree with the idea that simply trimming planning timelines and changing funding rules will automatically deliver affordable, good-quality homes. In Wales, I see communities paying the price when processes are rushed. Streamlining planning risks sacrificing environmental safeguards and local due process. When decisions are made quickly, essential infrastructure planning and biodiversity protections can be sidelined, leaving new developments with traffic and school capacity problems that we then struggle to fix. The Build-to-Rent approach may improve long-term rental stock, but without robust affordability covenants and professional management it can lock tenants into higher rents for longer and reduce opportunities for home ownership for young families. Reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing must come with strict, transparent obligations. In our area, viability exercises have been used to erode on-site affordable housing and infrastructure funding. A nearby station site was granted permission more than two years ago but remains idle, while rents climb and local schools strain. We need enforceable deals: on-site affordable homes or affordable receipts ring-fenced for local social housing, and capital for schools and roads. What would help more reliably: invest in council housing and genuinely affordable homes on public land, keep robust environmental safeguards, and require transparent, measurable delivery with penalties for non-delivery. Build-to-Rent should only be allowed with strong caps and clear long-term affordability.

From my point of view living in England, reforms should mix targeted demand measures with smart, supply-led actions that build on brownfield regeneration. I’d support pilots of rent stabilisation or caps aimed at genuinely affordable levels, but only with tight guardrails: time-limited schemes, clear sunset clauses, and robust evaluation on how they affect investment, landlord exit, maintenance quality and long-term supply. We need evidence from pilots before rolling out wide, to avoid squeezing the market and driving up neglect or disrepair.

Most of my area’s gains would come from regenerating underused sites rather than opening up green fields. Infill, conversions of vacant offices or shops, and refurbishing long-empty homes should be prioritised, with planning reforms that speed up legitimate schemes, and requirements for a meaningful portion of affordable homes. I’ve seen empty warehouses nearby that could become good-quality rental flats if barriers were lowered and funding targeted at retrofit and energy efficiency.

Alongside these, enable small and mid-sized builders and community-led housing with simpler processes and targeted grants or loans for decent standards, rather than just top-down mandates. Any expansion of concessions must hinge on solid evidence that quality remains high and that affordability genuinely improves, without harming the pipeline of new homes. Pilots and evaluations should be transparent and locally accountable.

From my experience in Wales, reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing as proposed would not automatically deliver more affordable, good-quality homes. In practice, developers often secure permission with off-site contributions or trimmed affordable housing through viability assessments; the promised on-site homes are rarely delivered on time or in the right places. I’ve seen a major project near my town where viability evidence reduced on-site affordable housing to a fraction of the target, and the infrastructure work that was meant to accompany it is still not in place after years. Local communities bear the burden of extra roads and schools before funds materialise.

I would rather see reforms that force enforceable, on-site affordable homes in every scheme, with fixed penalties if deadlines slip. Ensure CIL receipts are ring-fenced for local affordable housing and infrastructure, not diverted into general budgets, and subject to independent audit. Viability testing should be transparent, with independent appraisal and community input, not a shield for developers. Without stronger, enforceable obligations, these reforms risk simply enabling more planning permissions with little real benefit to people here who need genuinely affordable homes.

I strongly support reforms that streamline planning, zoning and decision timelines while keeping environmental safeguards. In my area in Scotland, well-located brownfield sites sit idle for years because the planning process drags on, with multiple rounds of consultation and inconsistent decisions between councils. A clearer, faster timetable would unlock supply while ensuring communities have proper input.

Specific reforms I’d back include: statutory decision deadlines for planning applications with automatic deemed consent if not decided on time; a single digital planning portal for applications, consultations and decisions; early pre-application engagement to resolve design and infrastructure issues before a formal submission; presumption of consent for minor affordable housing schemes on suitable sites; streamlined environmental assessment with standardised checks to avoid duplication but with robust safeguards; prioritisation of affordable and energy-efficient homes on brownfield land and infrastructure-led projects; and a cap on fees for small-scale affordable housing proposals.

In practice, these reforms would reduce uncertainty for builders and councils and speed up delivery of good-quality, energy-efficient homes for families like mine, while protecting the places we live and ensuring communities retain a voice.

absolutely from where I live in England, I’ve watched prices rise and affordable housing become ever more out of reach for ordinary families. I believe the most constructive reforms to increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes are those that bring land into play at sensible costs and ensure the uplift in land value from planning is reinvested locally in housing and infrastructure. Releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift through levies or taxes can work, but only if designed with clear rules, strong public accountability, and a focus on genuinely affordable outcomes.

First, release surplus public land quickly, but with explicit requirements for affordable homes and high-quality design. Public sites—things like unused council estates, former NHS facilities, or disused schools—should be prioritised for mixed-tenure housing. A robust target on public land could be something like a minimum of 40% affordable homes on such sites, with a balanced mix of social rent, affordable rent, and shared ownership. The remaining homes would be market housing to support viability, but the key is that the affordable element is protected in perpetuity and that new homes meet high standards of energy efficiency and accessibility. In practice, this would mean transparent land release criteria, a clear timetable, and a public-facing delivery plan so residents know when and where development will happen.

Second, capture planning uplift to fund affordable housing and local infrastructure through levies or taxes. The current system of planning obligations and developer contributions is tangled and slow, and the arrears can swallow the benefit of development. A more predictable uplift capture mechanism—be it a national Infrastructure Levy or a tightened, ring-fenced local planning gain—could ensure that the value added by rezoning or planning permission is reinvested in the very places that bore the costs of growth. I’d want a formula that guarantees a significant share of uplift goes directly to affordable housing and to infrastructure that serves new communities—schools, GP capacity, flood resilience, and reliable transport links. The revenue should be ring-fenced for the local area and quarterly reporting should show exactly what homes, how many, and at what price bands have been funded.

Third, ensure delivery is not compromised by bureaucracy or land-banking. A simpler, faster planning process paired with a well-staffed delivery arm in councils or allied bodies would help. Pre-approved design codes, brownfield-first zoning, and up-front infrastructure plans would accelerate delivery without sacrificing quality. It would also help to set up community land trusts or mutual housing models on some sites to keep prices closer to local incomes and to foster lasting community stewardship.

Fourth, maintain quality as a non-negotiable. New homes must be energy efficient, retrofit-ready, and accessible for different households over a lifetime. I’ve seen well-meaning developments that looked good on the plan but aged poorly in terms of energy performance and maintenance costs. The reforms should require Passivhaus or equivalent standards where feasible, embedded carbon reductions, and robust long-term management arrangements for communal spaces and green infrastructure.

Fifth, manage risks and protect local residents from displacement. Uplift capture should come with protections against price spikes in surrounding areas, and with strong anti-displacement measures for current residents. Local jobs targets in construction, local procurement rules, and measures to ensure that existing communities benefit from new investment will be essential to public acceptance and long-term sustainability.

In my area, there are several publicly owned plots that sit idle while families wait for a new affordable home or a better bus route to the town centre. A well-designed land-release and uplift-capture framework could turn those sites into affordable homes within a few years, with the funding also improving local infrastructure. I would also like to see pilots in a few wards to test how the revenue recycling works in practice—monitored, transparent, and published for residents to scrutinise.

Overall, I’m convinced the right combination of releasing public land and capturing planning uplift could unlock a steady stream of genuinely affordable homes while delivering quality builds and real improvements to local services. But it must be backed by clear targets, strict transparency, fast-track delivery, and strong protections for current residents. Used wisely, this approach could start to reverse the affordability crisis in communities like mine without sacrificing the character and sustainability of our towns and neighbourhoods!

Support reforms that prioritise more wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes for older people, students and key workers, including rural and cultural needs, plus higher energy standards for new builds and funded retrofits to cut bills and meet climate targets while protecting tenants and landlords from undue costs.

Living in England and renting in a city area, I see how high rents squeeze saving for a first home and affect my peers. I support exploring rent caps or stabilisation pilots as a way to improve affordability, provided they are properly designed and temporary, with robust evidence on impacts before rolling out nationally. A well‑structured pilot could limit annual rent increases for existing tenants to CPI plus a small corridor (for example CPI+1%), with exemptions for documented major capital works. Crucially, pilots should include protections to avoid sudden landlord exits and to maintain or raise property standards.

Alongside any cap, supply-side reforms are essential: allow faster planning and more release of public and infill land for purpose‑built rental, and ensure affordable units are delivered via Section 106 or new grants. Tie caps to measures of tenancy stability and property maintenance, so landlords invest in improvements rather than simply holding rents. Energy efficiency upgrades should be mandatory in funded schemes to cut bills and attract long-term tenants.

If evaluated carefully, pilots could show a balance between affordability and continued investment in quality homes for young people.

In our area, reforms should combine practical delivery with protections for places we value. First, we need more wheelchair‑accessible and adaptable homes, including older‑person schemes and supported living, plus student key‑worker housing near colleges and NHS facilities. I’d like to see a clear minimum—around 15–20% of affordable homes—built to wheelchair‑accessible standards with flexible layouts that can evolve for carers, home‑working or changing family needs. Design should be durable, with good insulation and energy efficiency, so costs stay affordable long term. 
Second, major public investment is welcome if it delivers genuinely affordable, long‑term social rents and is tied to solid, local governance. The funding should come with 20–30 year use‑and‑let models, strict rent caps related to local incomes, and guarantees on local job creation and supply chain apprenticeships. It should not be used to subsidise speculative market housing. 
Third, prioritise regeneration, infill and conversion of vacant and long‑empty homes before releasing Green Belt or greenfield land. In town centres we can convert vacant offices or mills into affordable flats and retrofit empty homes into energy‑efficient dwellings, preserving landscapes and reducing car dependence. 
Finally, streamline planning for small sites and brownfield redevelopments, with robust community benefit requirements and protections for countryside and ecosystems. These targeted reforms could lift supply without eroding what makes our area recognizable and loved.

As someone living in Scotland and navigating the rental market in my 30s, I’m convinced the best way to boost affordable, good-quality homes is to scale up purpose-built Build-to-Rent (BTR) and well-planned mixed-tenure schemes. When BTR projects include affordability covenants and strong, professional management, they don’t just add stock—they improve the whole rental experience: steadier rents, better maintenance, and longer-term neighbourhood stability. I’ve seen the contrast in blocks with active on-site management versus those left to private landlords who aren’t as responsive. The difference in upkeep, energy efficiency, and tenant wellbeing is palpable. We need reforms that make this approach the norm rather than the exception.

What reforms would make this work most effectively?

- Create a dedicated planning and delivery pathway for BTR and mixed-tenure schemes. In practice, that means fast-track, clearly defined planning routes for schemes that commit to affordability covenants and professional management, with decisions on major sites within a predictable timeframe (for example, a 12–16 week decision window after submission). By prioritising brownfield or derelict sites near good transport links, councils can unlock land that already has services and reduce pressures on greenfield areas.
- Use public land and land-use reform to kick-start long-term affordable rental stock. Where councils or public bodies have land suitable for housing, offer long-term leases to professional developers who commit to affordability covenants and to retain stock in rental tenure for the long term. A proportion of units should be secured as affordable for the long term (for example, a significant minority, such as 25–40%), with rents tethered to local affordability benchmarks. These covenants should endure for 15–30 years, giving tenants real security and enabling lenders to back the schemes with confidence.
- Mandate affordability covenants and cross-subsidy within schemes. Reforms should require that BTR developments include a mix of private rent and affordable units, with cross-subsidy mechanisms to fund initial capital costs while protecting long-term affordability. This approach helps deliver more units faster than relying on grant funding alone and ensures that the presence of affordable homes does not fade as the market tightens.
- Strengthen professional management and resident protections. Require on-site or locally based property management with responsive maintenance, energy-efficiency upgrades, and transparent service charges. Tenancies should offer longer security of tenure and predictable rent progression tied to local affordability indices, with caps on annual increases to prevent sudden spikes. Clear complaint avenues and timely remediation should be standard, not an afterthought.
- Raise building quality and energy standards. Set minimum standards for energy efficiency (ideally EPC B or higher) and high-quality designs that reduce long-term running costs. Homes should be well insulated, heat-pump compatible where suitable, and designed for climate resilience. This not only lowers bills for tenants but reduces voids caused by poor conditions.
- Plan for sustainable transport and community fit. New blocks should include adequate access to active travel networks and local services, with considerations for parking, green space, and public realm improvements. When communities feel they belong to a well-designed scheme, tenant turnover falls and cohesion rises.
- Establish transparent monitoring and accountability. Public reporting on how covenants are being maintained, how rents are set, and the condition of properties is essential. Tenant surveys, independent audits, and robust consumer protections should be built into the policy framework so schemes stay aligned with long-term affordability and quality goals.
- Encourage long-term partnerships between authorities, housing associations, and the private sector. A blended model that pairs public planning with private capital can deliver more quickly than pure market or pure social housing approaches. Supportive financing arrangements, such as guarantees or credit enhancements from the public sector, can reduce risk and lower debt costs, enabling more units to be built and retained as affordable housing.

From my day-to-day experience in Glasgow and surrounding areas, the upside is clear. When a block is managed professionally and designed with energy efficiency in mind, residents enjoy lower heat bills, fewer disputes, and more predictable housing costs. Neighbours feel more connected because there’s a stable community rather than a revolving door of tenants. In contrast, poorly maintained private lets create mistrust, more complaints, and higher turnover, which undermines local services and makes neighbourhoods feel less cohesive.

If these reforms are implemented, we’ll unlock a steady, high-quality supply of rental homes that families and workers can rely on. It’s not just about numbers; it’s about building durable places where people can put down roots, plan for the future, and contribute to their communities. I’d urge the government to prioritise BTR and mixed-tenure models with robust affordability covenants, professional management, and clear plans for local delivery in Scotland.

As a responding organisation representing young people in England, we disagree with reforms that prioritise housing supply without ensuring the accompanying services are funded and delivered in a timely, phased way. In practice, new developments often boast affordable homes but land on the infrastructure behind them: overcrowded schools, stretched GP surgeries, unrrliable bus services, and insufficient utilities. This undermines the quality of life and makes those homes less affordable in the long run. We urge reforms that require funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or even prior to housing. Key steps: - Create or strengthen a dedicated infrastructure fund and ensur levies and Section 106 money are ring-fenced and timed to housing phases,, not after. - Introduc service-readiness milestones linked to planning permissions, so housing cannot be completed without secure delivery dates for services. - Prioritise integrated transport and digital connectivity, with enough school places and local clinics to serve new communities. - Impose penalties for delays and provide incentives for earl delivery of services. From personal experience across estates in our area, these changes would stop the costly cycle of building and retrofitting and deliver affordable, good-quality homes that people can actually live in long-term.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. From our experience working with affordable housing initiatives in England, the most effective reforms will be those that fix the delivery pipeline: better local data and monitoring, stronger developer accountability, and significantly enhanced capacity within councils to plan, enforce, and deliver. I support reforms that make delivery more predictable and that ensure obligations attached to planning permissions actually materialise as affordable, good-quality homes for local people. At the same time, I want to stress that without resources and tough accountability, well-meaning rules will simply sit on the shelf or be gamed by clever viability arguments.

What we see on the ground in our area demonstrates the need for several linked changes:
- Large sites often promise a high share of affordable homes but face lengthy delays or changes in delivery commitments. Even where affordable units are counted at approval, completion lags behind schedule, or the units are reallocated to other schemes. In one current development, a Riverside quarter site promised around 40% affordable housing, yet after six years only a fraction had started, with a significant portion of funds and enforcement powers effectively in limbo. This erodes trust with local residents and reduces the impact of public investment.
- S106 and Community Infrastructure Levy money is sometimes earmarked for local needs (schools, GP surgeries, infrastructure) but the route to spend is opaque, and some allocated funds sit unused because delivery milestones are missed or planning enforcement is weak.
- Planning teams are overstretched in many councils, leading to delays in decision-making and in monitoring delivery post-approval. We’ve seen pockets of good practice, but the overall capacity to hold developers to account and to coordinate with housing associations and community land trusts is inconsistent.

Proposed reforms to increase supply and quality, with conditions for practical implementation:
- Real-time, public local housing delivery data: require councils to publish a transparent dashboard showing approvals, starts, completions, and actual affordable units delivered versus promised, with annual performance reports and clear timeframes. Data should be standardised across authorities to enable benchmarking and early flagging of under-delivery.
- Independent monitoring and robust enforcement: create an independent mechanism to audit delivery against planning commitments, including a clawback or step-in mechanism for when milestones aren’t met. If delivery slips, penalties should be triggered and funds redirected to accelerate delivery or fund alternative affordable homes. This should apply to both on-site delivery and transfer of affordable units into protected housing stock.
- Strengthen obligations on developers: require binding delivery plans as a condition of permission with explicit milestones and date-capped targets. Make viability assessments harder to weaponise by embedding clear tests for value extraction and ensuring affordable housing contributions are protected and not diminished through last-minute renegotiation.
- Fund planning, enforcement and delivery capacity: provide ring-fenced funding to councils to hire and retain planning officers, housing delivery staff, and enforcement agents. Invest in digital tools for casework management, pre-application advice, and rapid information exchange with developers and housing associations. Adequate capacity is essential to assess viability, monitor delivery, and take timely action when commitments slip.
- Accelerate on-site delivery and use of modern methods: expand permission for modular construction on suitable sites and on public land, with delivery milestones built into planning conditions. Streamline permission routes for small and medium-sized sites that prove viable, ensuring that the reduction in bureaucracy does not compromise quality.
- Use public land and community-led models: prioritise council and housing association-led delivery on surplus town or council land, including opportunities for community land trusts to maintain long-term affordability and local influence over design and management.
- Improve land supply clarity and timelines: address bottlenecks in land release, viability testing, and infrastructure provision so that sites with confirmed funding can progress without unnecessary delay. Clear, enforceable timelines for each phase of development will reduce speculative delays.
- Design quality and long-term stewardship: embed higher design quality standards and ensure that affordable homes are not only affordable to purchase or rent but also maintainable and durable for decades. Ensure long-term stewardship arrangements so that price stability and upkeep are preserved.
- Community engagement and transparency: maintain meaningful local involvement in design choices and ensure that affordable homes meet the needs of residents, including accessibility and suitability for different household types.

In short, reforms must couple tougher accountability with the capacity to act. The public sector cannot bear the risk of under-delivery alone, but with better data, a credible enforcement regime, and strengthened planning and delivery capacity, we can shift from promises on paper to real, affordable, good-quality homes being built and kept in communities. If these elements are implemented in a coordinated way, the gains could be substantial. Until then, the risk remains that many agreed affordable homes are not delivered or are delivered in ways that do not meet local need or long-term quality expectations.

Reforms that would actually boost affordable, good-quality homes in our area need to start with improving quality and stability in the rental market and making better use of existing stock, before opening the Green Belt to development. I would back: 1) stronger licensing and tougher enforcement for private landlords, with mandatory minimum standards for safety, energy efficiency, damp and repairs, plus penalties for neglect; 2) longer, secure tenancies with rent certainty and clear maintenance responsibilities, while ensuring small landlords are not bankrupted by red tape; 3) prioritising regeneration, infill and conversion of long-term empty buildings and vacant offices or shops, particularly in town centres, before any release of greenfield or Green Belt land; 4) support for purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management to deliver high-quality long-term rental stock you can rely on.

In my area we have derelict mills and empty shops that could be converted into affordable flats if planning, viability and licensing allow it; a robust approach here would also tackle defects in existing stock, improving energy efficiency and safety. Only then should Green Belt release be considered, and only at sites proven to deliver genuinely affordable homes.

I live in England and am responding as an individual. My family has felt the impact of rising energy costs and the challenge of finding good-quality, affordable homes in my area. I want reforms that make not just more homes, but better homes that are affordable to run and fit for the long term. In particular I support measures to raise energy standards for new builds and to fund retrofits, alongside clearer, enforceable planning obligations that deliver on-site affordable housing and the right infrastructure in sync with housing growth.

First, tightening energy standards for new homes is essential. Mandating higher energy performance for all new builds will cut bills for tenants and owners and help us meet climate targets without simply shifting costs from one group to another. The most practical approach is to make the Future Homes Standard the default rather than a optional extra, and to combine that with delivery of low-carbon heating and robust insulation, airtightness, and heat-loss standards. When new homes are genuinely energy-efficient, the ongoing cost of heating and maintaining them is lower, which makes them genuinely affordable in practice. I also welcome a national, well-funded retrofit program so existing homes can be upgraded—especially for households on lower incomes and for social housing stock. In our area, many homes suffer from poor insulation and drafty rooms, and the winter bills are a heavy burden. Government funding that helps landlords and homeowners install insulation, draught-proofing, heat pumps, or district heating can make a real difference in monthly outlays and in the comfort and health of households.

Second, reforming Section 106, CIL and viability testing with greater transparency and enforceable obligations is critical. Developers should contribute fairly to the local infrastructure and to affordable homes, and that money should be predictable and verifiable. The current landscape can feel inconsistent from borough to borough, and viability assessments can be used to erode on-site affordable provision after a scheme is approved. What’s needed is a standardised, independently validated viability framework with published assumptions and clear thresholds. When a project is viable with a substantial contribution to affordable housing and infrastructure, that obligation should be secured on-site and time-limited with firm delivery milestones. 

In practice, I’d like to see:
- A robust baseline of affordable housing on-site funded through S106 contributions, with a default expectation of, for example, a significant percentage of homes delivered as on-site affordable housing in suitable schemes, unless there are demonstrable, agreed exceptions with independent oversight.
- A transparent CIL framework, with a clear portion ring-fenced for local housing and infrastructure needs (schools, roads, flood defences, GP capacity, and parks). Local authorities would publish how funds are allocated and the expected delivery timelines.
- An independent, consistently applied viability assessment process, with published methodologies, so developers can’t game the system and communities can see how decisions are reached.
- Timely decisions for schemes that deliver affordable housing and energy-efficient homes, with predictable conditions and realistic build-out plans. This would reduce delays that often stall projects and push costs onto renters.

A concrete example from our area helps illustrate why these reforms matter. A recent housing proposal promised a good mix of homes and on-site affordable housing, but after viability testing, the affordable portion was dramatically reduced and there was little certainty about when or how those homes would be delivered. If there were a standard, transparent viability test and enforceable on-site obligations, communities would have confidence that growth translates into genuinely affordable homes in a timely way, not just a headline figure that disappears down a back room somewhere.

Finally, I’d stress that reforms must protect tenants and landlords from disproportionate upfront costs while still delivering energy efficiency. Higher standards for new builds should be paired with grants or low-interest loans for retrofits and with long-term planning that keeps rents affordable. By aligning energy efficiency, housing supply, and infrastructure funding through clear, transparent rules, we can build more affordable, good-quality homes that are not only affordable to rent or buy today but are affordable to run for years to come.

Please implement these reforms in a coherent package: raise energy standards for new builds, fund retrofits, and reform S106/CIL/viability with transparency and enforceable obligations. That combination can unlock more affordable homes, improve living standards, and support climate goals without piling costs onto tenants or stifling development.

In Wales, the shortage of affordable, good‑quality homes is felt across towns and valleys alike. If we want more homes, reforms must help local builders win work and build to high standards without jeopardising viability.

- Targeted finance and procurement access: create ring‑fenced finance for SME builders, and local procurement frameworks that reserve a portion of public contracts for smaller firms. Provide dedicated support through pre‑planning advice and shorter procurement routes, and incentivise councils to release land for small‑site development rather than only large schemes.
- Small‑sites policy and planning support: make it easier to bring forward 20–50 unit schemes on brownfield and surplus public land, with fast‑track planning and clear, consistent expectations. Local authorities should be given the resources to provide hands‑on planning guidance and to de‑risk small sites, so local builders can compete and scale up.
- Licensing, enforcement, minimum quality standards and longer tenancies: strengthen licensing and enforcement to curb rogue landlords, raise minimum decency and energy efficiency standards, and promote longer tenancies with appropriate protections. Pair this with incentives (grants, tax relief, longer amortisation) to maintain viability for small landlords who supply decent homes.
- Energy standards: I’m wary of a blanket mandate for higher energy standards on all new builds if it raises costs and slows supply. Support a staged, needs‑based approach with retrofit funding to reduce bills and meet climate targets, ensuring upgrades are affordable for tenants and landlords alike.

In my area, a local SME builder explained that easier land release, finance, and planning support could unlock several small sites a year and deliver affordable homes without compromising quality.

Affordable homes are vital in our area. I agree that reforms are needed to genuinely increase supply while keeping rents fair. A careful set of rent-stabilisation pilots could help households with low to middle incomes sit comfortably, without destabilising the market. I would support a scheme where caps are evidence-based, regionally calibrated, sunset after 3-5 years, and paired with rigorous evaluation to track effects on new builds, landlord exits, and maintenance investment. If pilots show that supply remains healthy, we can scale up; if not, we adjust quickly.

We also need more wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes and dedicated stock for older people, supported housing and student key-worker housing. In practice, this means guaranteeing a portion of all new developments is fully accessible, and funding for adaptable interiors that can flex over a family's life cycle. It would help rural communities if planning reforms incentivised development near transport hubs and essential services, and if there was targeted funding for purpose-built homes for key workers, including NHS and education staff near workplaces.

In short, combine principled rent reform pilots with ambitious, targeted supply standards and planning reforms to unlock a diverse, quality, affordable pipeline.

REFORM TARGETED FINANCE AND PROCUREMENT ACCESS TO HELP SME AND LOCAL BUILDERS UNLOCK DIVERSE, LOCAL HOUSING, ESPECIALLY VIA SMALL-SITES POLICY AND PLANNING SUPPORT. I WOULD ALSO PRIORITISE REGENERATION, INFILL AND CONVERSIONS OF VACANT/EMPTY HOMES BEFORE RELEASING GREENFIELD OR GREEN BELT LAND TO PROTECT LANDSCAPES.

As an organisation operating across England, we strongly support reform of Section 106, the Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) and viability testing, with greater transparency and enforceable obligations to secure on-site affordable homes and infrastructure funding. Clear, binding delivery requirements help ensure affordable homes are built where they are most needed and connected to schools, healthcare and transport, rather than being delayed or waived. Transparent viability assessments protect affordable outcomes and stop late-stage value engineering reducing the promised on-site provision. This approach would speed up delivery and give local communities confidence in development plans. We also back targeted provision of wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes and dedicated streams for older people, supported housing and student key-worker housing, designed to reflect demographic, rural realities and cultural needs. Practical features—lift-access in low-rise blocks, flexible layouts for changing family needs, step-free entrances, and proximity to public transport and services—should be standard. In our projects, integrating these elements with on-site affordable housing and robust infrastructure funding reduces churn, supports social inclusion and delivers genuinely affordable, good-quality homes for diverse households.

From my place in England, as a retiree, I welcome reforms that improve local data, monitoring, developer accountability and fund council planning, enforcement and delivery capacity to ensure commitments are delivered. In my area, too many schemes promised affordable homes that then stalled or were re-priced as market units. A robust, publicly accessible data dashboard showing planned, started and completed homes, plus the percentage of affordable units and their tenure, would help councils and residents hold developers to account. A dedicated delivery team within the council, supported by ring-fenced funding and clear penalties for non-delivery, would reduce delays and improve quality on site. On the ground, authorities could require independent quality checks before handover. 

I also support strengthening licensing and enforcement and promoting longer tenancies, while balancing measures to protect small landlords’ viability. Longer tenancies provide security for families and neighbours, reducing displacement, but licensing must be affordable and straightforward; consider phased implementation and grants for essential safety upgrades to avoid driving up rents or driving owners out of the market.

Together, these reforms could boost supply of affordable, good-quality homes while keeping outcomes fair for landlords and tenants alike.

I welcome the government’s focus on reforms to increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes. For me, the quickest and most lasting way to boost supply is to empower community‑led housing models—community land trusts, housing co‑operatives, self‑build projects and the use of modern methods of construction (MMC). These approaches can deliver genuinely affordable homes that are well designed, energy efficient and locally accountable, while also helping to unlock sites that the market alone struggles to bring forward.

In our area, families and young people are finding it harder to get a foothold. Private rents have risen steeply and social housing queues are long. I’ve spoken to neighbours who would consider living in a self‑build or a small cooperative project if the process wasn’t so unclear and costly. There is real appetite locally for a CLT‑led development near the town centre and a few derelict sites in the surrounding villages look ripe for community‑led reuse. If a pilot CLT model could acquire such land at sensible cost and manage it for long‑term affordability, it could deliver a mix of affordable rent and affordable ownership in three to five years, rather than the decades that sometimes follow large speculative developments.

What reforms would help most:

- Make land available to community groups at realistic prices and protect it from speculative use. Local councils and landowners should be able to offer surplus public land to CLTs or co‑ops at discounted rates, with long‑term stewardship tied to affordable outcomes. Designating a clear proportion of suitable sites in local plans for community‑led housing—with a fast‑track planning route and reduced upfront delays—would dramatically speed things up. Evidence from CLT projects elsewhere shows that long‑term stewardship can keep rents affordable across generations, not just for the first occupants.

- Streamline planning and procurement for community‑led schemes. A dedicated, predictable planning framework for CLTs and housing co‑ops, including standardised neighbour consultation and design guidelines, would reduce time and cost. Local authorities should be encouraged to reserve a share of land or planning obligations on larger sites for community‑led housing and to pre‑qualify community groups so they can bid on sites with confidence.

- Improve access to patient, affordable finance and reduce up‑front costs. A national fund or guarantee scheme to support the initial set‑up costs of CLTs and co‑ops, plus low‑interest development loans, would lower the barrier to forming community groups. Flexible mortgage products for self‑build and custom‑build homes—when under the umbrella of a community group—would help families realise plans more quickly.

- Support self‑build and modular construction. Simplifying some of the planning and build‑phase requirements for self‑build and group self‑build projects would unlock more local, hands‑on participation. Government backing for MMC pilots—e.g., modular timber frames or off‑site manufactured panels—could reduce on‑site time, improve quality, and achieve higher energy performance at similar or lower costs. In my conversations with colleagues and neighbours, many people would prefer a home built to modern standards that is adaptable for changing needs over a long lifetime.

- Strengthen quality and energy standards through MMC. Requiring high energy efficiency in new affordable homes—targeting near‑zero emissions where feasible—and using proven MMC technologies helps keep running costs down and ensures homes stay affordable for decades. It should come with robust warranties and clear maintenance responsibilities for community groups to avoid long‑term management issues.

- Build capacity and maintain accountability. Providing governance training, legal clarity on land ownership structures (leasehold vs. freehold), and ongoing maintenance funding helps community groups stay sustainable. Regular reporting on how many homes are delivered, the mix of affordable rents and ownership, and energy performance would help communities see progress and keep faith in these models.

From my own experience and by talking with local residents, I’ve seen how quickly a well‑led CLT or co‑op can mobilise around a site, engage the community, and deliver homes that families can afford now and enjoy for generations. When I visited another town where a small CLT was piloting a 12‑home site on a former garage site, the planning process was noticeably smoother once a local authority had a dedicated community‑led housing officer and a clear timetable. The homes were designed with good daylight, solid insulation, and low running costs—features we know matter once people move in and stay long term.

If these reforms are implemented, they would complement market delivery while ensuring higher quality design, long‑term affordability, and faster delivery in my area. I’m convinced that enabling CLTs, co‑ops, self‑build and MMC—supported by sensible land, finance and planning reforms—can help us move from waiting lists to genuinely affordable homes people are proud to live in.

Thank you for considering these approaches; I hope they are given priority in the next round of housing reforms.

I disagree with approaches that prioritise short-term tax breaks for Buy-to-Let or simply releasing more land without strong affordability protections. In my view, the most effective reform is to accelerate purpose-built Build‑to‑Rent and mixed‑tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management to boost long‑term rental supply. These schemes create stable, long‑term homes for renters, with on‑site management, responsive maintenance, and predictable rents. Mixed tenure ensures communities aren’t divided into all private rentals or all owner‑occupiers. Affordability covenants keep a portion of units affordable in perpetuity, rather than a one‑off discount. In practice, when I’ve rented in a newer BTR block, I’ve benefited from longer tenancy terms, clear repairs routines, and better insulation and energy efficiency, simply because there’s a professional landlord who can’t walk away. To scale this, planning rules should require BTR and mixed‑tenure on big sites, with robust affordability covenants, and local authorities empowered to enforce quality standards. If we can lock in long‑term rents and proper management, we’ll ease the pressure on all renters and reduce the churn that harms communities.

it's outrageous that i welcome the reforms proposed to increase the supply of affordable, good-quality homes in England, and I’m glad there’s an explicit link made between housing and the essential services that make a community work. In practice, I believe we should require funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside—or even ahead of—new housing. If new homes arrive without reliable access to buses, safe routes to schools, GP capacity and robust utilities, they risk becoming unsustainable dormitory suburbs, which just pushes problems down the line rather than solving them.

From my experience in our area, developments have often moved faster than the infrastructure to support them. A recent estate added hundreds of affordable and private homes, but the new bus routes and rail connections were only announced much later, and GP appointments were already booked up well beyond what the new residents expected. Parents faced longer school queues and crowded classrooms, while existing residents worried about pressure on local services that were already stretched. It isn’t enough to simply set targets for the number of homes; you have to guarantee the services that allow those homes to function well from day one, and to scale them in step with population growth.

So how should these reforms work in practice? First, we need masterplans that require infrastructure to be funded and secured before or in tandem with housing. This means a statutory framework where transport, schools, healthcare, broadband and utilities funding is attached to planning consent, with clear delivery timetables. Second, infrastructure should be phased in lockstep with housing—each new tranche of homes should come with a commensurate package of transport capacity, school places, and healthcare access, not as an afterthought. Third, there must be robust funding mechanisms: ring-fenced government contributions, accountable developer contributions aligned to actual delivery, and, where appropriate, long-term public-private partnerships to underwrite major improvements like road upgrades or new rail links.

Local accountability is essential. Independent oversight should monitor progress against agreed milestones, with penalties or alternative delivery arrangements if facilities fall behind. I’d also like to see a focus on value capture to fund future-needed infrastructure and a guaranteed minimum proportion of affordable homes that remain genuinely affordable for local people, not just a one-off planning gain.

Another practical step is prioritising brownfield sites with existing infrastructure, but only if the surrounding services can be upgraded to meet demand. That means ensuring upgrades to water and sewer capacity, electricity grids, and reliable broadband, as well as safe walking and cycling routes that connect to town centres and stations. Good design matters too: energy-efficient homes, flood-resilient layouts, good public spaces and access to green amenities all help communities thrive.

I am in my early sixties and I’m thinking about the long-term viability of our area. The reforms should protect local services for everyone, not just new residents, and they should be planned with input from communities, schools, health partners and transport operators. If these reforms are implemented with proper funding and clear phasing, new developments can bring affordable homes and strengthen the local economy, while preserving the character and quality of life that people in our area value.

Overall, I support reforms that put service readiness at the heart of housing delivery, because only then will affordable, good-quality homes really be sustainable for the long term!

I’d favour reforms that combine better access to finance for SME and local builders with targeted investment to deliver genuinely affordable social rented homes. In our area the biggest blockers are finance for modest-site developments and the planning process, which can feel unpredictable for small firms. A small-sites policy that frees up 5–40 home plots on brownfield land, plus streamlined pre-application guidance and reduced planning risk, would help a wider range of local builders bring voices and jobs into neighbourhoods. Procurement should include local SME quotas, simpler bid requirements, and multi-year frameworks to give firms genuine certainty. Public funds should back high-quality, energy-efficient standards and support community-led housing models, not just volume outputs.

At the same time there’s a clear need for major public investment in council and housing association programmes to deliver genuinely affordable, long-term social rented homes for low-income households. The challenge is funding and maintenance over the long term, so rents stay affordable and stock remains well cared for. A blended approach could work if there is a ring-fenced revenue stream and guarantees that social rents are preserved even as the market develops.

Practical reforms could include a mortgage-guarantee fund for small-site lending, planning reforms to cut delays, and dedicated acquisition funds for locally led schemes that prioritise quality and affordability.

From my experience renting in an English town, more homes alone won’t secure affordability or quality. Reforms that actively promote purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes, with affordability covenants and professional on-site management, could expand long-term rental supply and lift living standards.

Key reforms:
- Planning: streamline approvals for mid-rise BTR in town centres; require 20-30% of units to stay affordable via long-term covenants; ensure infrastructure contributions are timely.
- Affordability: index rents to local earnings with caps on renewals; offer 10- to 20-year tenancies with predictable increases tied to local wages.
- Management: on-site managers, clear service-charge rules, prompt repairs, and energy-efficiency upgrades to lower bills.
- Oversight: annual reporting on occupancy and covenant compliance; local authorities empowered to enforce terms.

Personal note: a nearby BTR block with professional management kept shared areas tidy and replies quick, but renewal rents later exceeded local wages. A robust covenant framework would help anchor affordability while preserving the benefits of professional management.

it's outrageous that in our area, the housing market feels like a squeeze on both rents and bills, especially for pensioners and households on modest incomes. I believe the reforms that will most effectively increase affordable, good-quality homes are those that raise energy standards for new builds and fund retrofits across existing housing stock. When homes are built to high energy efficiency standards, fuel bills stay down for tenants and owners, and the upfront construction costs are offset over time by lower running costs. The retrofit funding, targeted at both social housing and private rentals, would avoid placing disproportionate costs on tenants or small landlords while delivering warmer, more affordable homes sooner.

For new builds, I would like to see a clear, enforceable requirement that all new homes meet strong energy performance standards. This could include: robust insulation (roofs, walls, floors), airtight construction to reduce heat loss, and the integration of low-carbon heating, such as heat pumps, where suitable, with measured efficiency upgrades like better glazing and high-efficiency boilers. It isn’t enough to say “build greener”; we must back it with practical requirements and clear timelines so developers plan ahead rather than push costs onto tenants later. If standards are phased in with financial support for builders during the transition, the market can adapt without slowing the overall supply of homes.

Equally important is funding for retrofits. Many local residents live in older, poorly insulated homes that leak heat and push up bills during cold winters. A nationwide retrofit programme, delivered through councils and housing associations, could offer grants or low-interest loans to cover insulation, draught-proofing, and upgrades to efficient heating systems. In my street, a couple of neighbours have damp, poorly insulated terraces; even small improvements—loft insulation, wall insulation, modern boilers—would noticeably cut their annual bills. If funding is designed to cover a substantial share of the cost—ideally 50–70% for the least able households—more homes can be upgraded without creating new rent burdens for tenants.

Delivery should be practical and local. The plan should fund training for tradespeople and create local jobs so the work is done quickly and to a high standard. I’ve seen how delays in the supply chain and a shortage of skilled workers hold back beneficial upgrades in our area. A policy that supports a steady stream of competent installers, backed by public procurement and incentives for quality work, would help avoid delays and ensure good workmanship. We should also use modern construction methods where appropriate to speed up new-build delivery while maintaining quality and durability.

Planning and funding together can also increase the affordable-housing supply. Reforms to streamline planning for small-to-medium sites, with a requirement for a reasonable share of affordable homes in new developments, would add to the overall stock. Rebalancing contributions from developers so that a portion goes toward energy-efficient renovations and affordable rentals could ensure the benefits are shared widely, not limited to those who can pay a premium for new-builds.

To measure success, there should be simple, transparent targets and regular reporting on energy performance, housing quality, and affordability outcomes. Sanctions for non-compliant landlords and timely enforcement will be important so standards are not mere promises on paper.

As someone living on a fixed income, I know bills are a constant worry. If we can deliver higher energy standards in new homes and a robust retrofit programme—at scale and with proper support—the result will be warmer homes, lower bills, and fewer households pushed into fuel poverty. It also moves us closer to meeting climate targets in a fair way, without loading extra costs onto tenants or small landlords who already face tight margins.

I disagree that reforms to Section 106, CIL and viability testing alone will most effectively increase the supply of affordable, good‑quality homes in our area. Greater transparency and enforceable obligations are welcome, but without a broader package they risk not delivering real on‑site affordable homes. 

In practice, viability testing can still be used to shrink affordable shares or delay delivery, and I’ve seen schemes in our town where promised affordable units disappeared after viability assessments and no timely delivery followed. Reforming the system without other measures could push costs into rents or house prices, harming young renters like those in my cohort. 

What would work better locally is a package of reforms: (1) ring‑fenced, transparent S106/CIL contributions with binding deadlines for on‑site delivery or timely, close‑by off‑site delivery; (2) independent, standardised viability checks with public reporting; (3) faster planning routes for publicly owned land and for genuinely affordable housing; (4) direct public investment in social/affordable housing, including borrowing powers for local authorities; (5) support for community‑led models like community land trusts; (6) clearer, more realistic definitions of what counts as affordable. 

We need action that directly builds homes and guarantees affordability, not just new reporting requirements.

Experience in my area has shown that simply accelerating housing construction without service readiness creates new pressures on households. Reforms that focus only on unlocking land or speeding planning will not deliver affordable, good-quality homes unless they are paired with funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside or before housing. I live in England and have seen new estates go up while the roads are still congested, the nearest GP is at capacity, and school places are limited. 

A credible reform would attach infrastructure milestones to housing delivery: fund bus route upgrades or new services when every 500 homes are completed; guarantee a new school block when occupancy reaches a certain threshold; expand the local health centre and upgrades to water, energy and broadband as homes are brought online. Developers could contribute through a ring-fenced infrastructure fund, with councils enforcing milestones before completions proceed. 

Without this, affordable homes end up in places with poor transport links, stretched services and higher living costs, which undermines affordability and sustainability. My own experience with longer commutes and difficulty getting GP appointments after a new estate opened reinforces that service readiness must be integral, not optional, to any reform.

Living in England, I strongly support reforms to increase affordable, good‑quality homes. Major public investment in council and housing association building programmes is essential to deliver genuinely affordable, long‑term social rented homes for low‑income households. In my area, private development often fails to provide homes people can actually afford, leaving families stuck in overcrowded private rentals. A sustained programme funded and delivered by councils and housing associations would provide secure homes, reduce homelessness, and help stabilise communities. 

I also back innovative and faster routes such as community land trusts, co‑operatives, self‑build and modern methods of construction. CLTs can steward land for lasting affordability, and housing co‑ops give residents a say in management while keeping rents low. In our town, a local CLT is exploring land for 12 affordable homes; a small co‑op is piloting modular flats that could be delivered more quickly while maintaining quality. Modern methods of construction, with strict quality and ongoing maintenance funding, could dramatically raise supply without compromising standards. 

Reforms should include ring‑fenced funding for social housing, streamlined planning with affordable‑housing quotas, land release for non‑profit builders, and access to long‑term public borrowing for councils.

i strongly believe i live in England and want more affordable, good-quality homes, but reforms that rely mainly on more private-sector targets won't deliver unless we fix the bottlenecks in data, accountability and local delivery capacity. In my area the planning department is chronically under-resourced; we see planning permission granted but sites stall because there aren't enough officers to manage the delivery and enforcement.

What would help most: real-time local housing delivery data published publicly—starts, completions, affordable units, and performance against milestones for major sites. Independent monitoring of progress, with clear consequences if developers miss deadlines; penalties, or requirement to fund remedial work if delays push up costs or leave people waiting.

Fund council planning and enforcement capacity: ring-fenced funding to recruit skilled planners, case officers, and building-control staff, plus modern case-management and digital tracking so residents can see progress.

Make commitments legally binding and enforceable: ensure Section 106 agreements and affordable housing contributions are delivered on time; apply long-stop dates and clawback if missed, rather than letting schemes stall.

Also ensure early investment in infrastructure to unlock sites—schools, roads, and public transport—so homes are truly affordable in practice.

From experience, without stronger local governance and data, many promised homes simply never appear. These reforms would likely shift the balance toward delivery!

From our organisation representing residents across this area, I welcome the debate on affordable housing. Yet I fear that focusing mainly on the volume of new homes risks overlooking what actually helps people here. The largest issues we encounter are the backlog of maintenance in older affordable stock and the high cost of energy, which erodes what little income families have left for rent. A credible reform should prioritise retrofit and energy efficiency as a route to real affordability, rather than just counting new builds. Local data show about 1,200 households on waiting lists, with around a third needing adaptable or accessible homes. Planning and approvals on brownfield sites can drag delivery out by 12–18 months, especially where lift- and staircase-accessible flats are involved. Small- to medium-sized builders report that stable, long-term funding and guarantees for affordable rents would unlock more delivery than subsidies aimed only at volume.

In short, reforms should balance quantity with quality, ensure accessibility and sustainability, and support community-led models that keep homes affordable in the long term for families and older residents alike.

I disagree with broad rent-cap reforms; pilots are needed to test impacts on supply and landlord exit, as cap could deter investment. Also reform Section 106/CIL with clear, enforceable on-site affordable housing and infrastructure funding requirements.

I support reforms that deliver more wheelchair-accessible, adaptable homes for older people, supported housing, and student key-worker housing, especially in rural and culturally diverse areas. Releasing surplus public land and capturing planning uplift via levies could reduce land costs and fund housing and local infrastructure.

absolutely prices in my area have crept up faster than wages for several years, and I’ve watched friends and colleagues struggle to find good-quality homes that won’t break the bank. I’d like reforms that unlock a steady pipeline of affordable, well-made homes while avoiding the kind of bottlenecks that push projects off track. I’m supportive of a mix of approaches that can bring in community leadership, better construction methods, and sensible price controls where needed. In short: empower community-led schemes, make modern construction work in practice, and pilot targeted rent stability to keep housing affordable while protecting supply.

Community land trusts (CLTs) and housing co-operatives offer a practical path to affordable, high-quality homes with a local stake and long-term stewardship. If local land is owned by a community land trust, the homes can be rented or sold at genuinely affordable levels in perpetuity, insulated from speculative swings. This also helps keep development decisions aligned with local needs—schools, transport, and green space can be planned around a trusted, local model. In our region, a CLT could unlock a small brownfield site on which 40–60 homes could be delivered with long leases to ensure affordability for families and first-time buyers who would otherwise be priced out of the market. Housing co-ops, run by residents with a democratic voice, can deliver excellent standards of maintenance and energy efficiency, while keeping rents predictable and transparent. I’d welcome dedicated support for these models: land reform that releases public or unused land for CLTs, patient finance for start-up costs, and a simple regulatory route so communities can get projects off the ground without endless red tape.

Self-build and modern methods of construction (MMC) have clear potential to accelerate supply and raise quality. Self-build lets households tailor homes to their needs, while MMC—modular timber frames, panelised systems, factory-built components—reduces on-site waste, shortens construction times, and can deliver better energy performance. In our area, I’ve spoken to developers who’ve used modular techniques for social housing projects; the speed and quality were noticeably better, but the upfront costs and planning requirements still slowed things down. If the government can provide scalable financing and adopt pre-approved MMC designs for small sites, we could unlock quicker delivery on land that is otherwise considered marginal. A combined approach—reserve land for community-led or small-build MMC projects, with finance that supports high quality, long-term maintenance—would mean homes go up faster, and stay affordable longer.

Planning and land-release reforms should align with these aims. I’d support a policy toolkit that makes it easier for community-led groups to buy land or lease long-term, with clear, predictable planning routes for small sites and schemes that include a social-tenure mix. On larger developments, require a meaningful proportion of affordable homes and ease the process for CLTs or co-ops to participate through pre-approved designs and streamlined planning conditions. Prioritising brownfield sites and public land where affordable housing is the primary objective would send a strong signal that housing policy is about people, not just numbers.

I’m also open to rent caps or stabilization pilots as part of a measured approach to affordability, provided they’re evidence-based and carefully designed to avoid undermining supply. A limited, well-monitored pilot—applied to selected areas for, say, 3–5 years—could help determine whether caps prevent displacement while still encouraging investment and maintenance. Caps could be set below market rents and tied to local incomes or inflation, with protections for legitimate landlords and small-scale private landlords to avoid a sudden withdrawal from the market. It’s crucial that pilots include robust data collection on rental turnover, new build activity, investment levels, and the condition of properties. If, after evaluation, pilots show negative impacts on supply, the policy should be adjusted rather than rolled out nationally. If they demonstrate improved affordability without harming quality or new investment, they could form a cautious, evidence-based part of a wider reform package.

Taken together, these reforms would help deliver more affordable, high-quality homes near jobs and services—homes that stay affordable and that communities can take pride in. The key is real choice: CLTs and housing co-ops for long-term affordability and local control; MMC and self-build to speed up supply and improve quality; planning reform to reduce unnecessary friction; and carefully evaluated rent-stability pilots to smooth affordability pressures without choking off investment. If the government combines funding, clear rules, and strong local partnerships, we can see significant, lasting improvements in the supply of affordable homes in our area while maintaining high standards of quality and energy efficiency.

England needs more affordable, high-quality homes with speed. We support reforms that unlock community land trusts, housing co-operatives, self-build and modern methods of construction to bring down costs and speed up delivery. In our area, a community land trust with a shared equity model could hold land in trust, preventing spiralling prices and ensuring homes stay affordable for the long term. Co-ops can preserve high standards and give residents a stake in management. Self-build and modular construction have shown faster completion with better energy efficiency, reducing bills for older tenants.

We also back stronger licensing, enforcement and minimum quality standards, and promoting longer tenancies to provide stability for families and retirees alike, while ensuring small landlords remain viable through sensible regulation and support.

Encouraging purpose-built Build-to-Rent and mixed-tenure schemes with affordability covenants and professional management would grow the long-term rental stock and maintenance quality. In a recent nearby development, Build-to-Rent has delivered well-managed homes with predictable rents.

Please support planning reforms and targeted funding to scale these routes, ensuring local suitability, high-quality design and energy efficiency.

I strongly support major public investment in council and housing association building programmes to deliver genuinely affordable, long-term social rented homes for low-income households. In our area, private rents have risen sharply and available social housing is the only reliable route to stability for families on modest incomes. Having myself seen a younger couple on the local housing list stuck in nightly temp accommodation for months, I know how crucial secure, affordable renting is for children’s schooling and older relatives’ care. A well-funded public programme can use modern, energy-efficient construction and long-term planning to keep costs down for tenants. It would also create skilled local jobs and reduce reliance on speculative developers. I’d like to see transparent procurement, strong tenancy protections, and a mix of new flats and family-sized homes to meet different needs. Public investment must be long-term and shielded from political cycles, with guarantees on maintenance and tenancy security. This approach would stabilise communities and prevent more households falling into costly private-rented cycles.

Reforms should require funded, phased provision of transport, schools, healthcare and utilities alongside housing, or before it, to make new communities truly service-ready. With that infrastructure-led approach and targeted subsidies or land-value tools, affordable, good-quality homes could be more reliably delivered.

Strongly support reforms that unlock more affordable, good‑quality homes through a mix of big‑scale public investment and smarter use of land.
